parts.instr: Listen to a talk about a tool library and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe bài nói về một thư viện dụng cụ và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the monthly meeting of the Eastfield Community Association. I'm Priya, and tonight I'd like to tell you about our tool library.

The idea came from my neighbor, who bought an expensive drill for one small job and then never used it again. Many of us own tools that sit in garages for years, so we thought, why not share them? We began three years ago with just forty tools in a church hall. Today we have over two thousand tools and about six hundred members.

Membership is simple. It costs twelve dollars a year, with a reduced rate of six dollars for people over sixty-five. You can borrow up to three items at a time. We have everything from saws to sewing machines, but the most popular item by far is the ladder, followed closely by the lawn mower. Garden tools go out especially fast in spring.

You can keep a tool for one week. If you need it for longer, you can renew it once, but no more than that. When you first join, please bring a bill that shows your home address. We don't need a photo ID or a bank card.

Our main building is on Park Road and is open from ten to four on weekdays. Next month we open a second branch at the Westgate Library, which has much more space than the church hall had. We rely on volunteers. A few of them repair broken tools, but most spend their time helping members choose the right tool for a job and showing them how to use it safely.

On Saturday mornings we run free workshops. This term the topic is basic bicycle repair, and next term it will be woodworking. Finally, our plan for next year is to add a section of kitchen equipment, such as cake mixers and pasta makers. We also thought about camping equipment, but storing tents would take too much room. Thank you for listening, and now I'll take your questions.

items.q: How did the idea for the tool library start?
options: A neighbor bought a drill and hardly used it.
A member of the association visited a similar library abroad.
The church wanted to use its hall for a new project.
items.vi: Ý tưởng bắt nguồn từ người hàng xóm mua máy khoan đắt tiền rồi ít dùng.

items.q: How many members does the library have now?
items.vi: Có hơn 2.000 dụng cụ nhưng chỉ khoảng 600 thành viên.

items.q: How much does membership cost for people over sixty-five?
items.vi: Mức phí giảm cho người trên 65 tuổi là 6 đô la một năm.

items.q: Which item is borrowed most often?
items.vi: Thang là món được mượn nhiều nhất, máy cắt cỏ đứng ngay sau.

items.q: How long can a member keep a tool without renewing it?
items.vi: Mỗi dụng cụ được giữ một tuần, chỉ gia hạn được một lần.

items.q: What must new members bring when they join?
items.vi: Thành viên mới cần mang hóa đơn có địa chỉ, không cần ảnh ID.

items.vi: Chi nhánh thứ hai sẽ mở tại thư viện Westgate vào tháng sau.

options: help members choose and use tools
items.vi: Phần lớn tình nguyện viên giúp thành viên chọn và dùng dụng cụ an toàn.

items.q: What is the topic of the Saturday workshops this term?
items.vi: Học kỳ này là sửa xe đạp, học kỳ sau mới là làm đồ gỗ.

items.vi: Kế hoạch năm sau là thêm dụng cụ nhà bếp, đồ cắm trại bị loại vì tốn chỗ.

parts.instr: Listen to two students talking to their tutor and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe hai sinh viên trao đổi với gia sư và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, let's talk about your project on noise in open-plan offices. Lena, remind me why you chose this topic.

Well, Marcus's sister works in an open-plan office, and she was always complaining that she couldn't concentrate. We found plenty of studies that measured noise levels, but very few that asked people how they actually feel.
Right. That seemed like a real gap in the research.
Good, that's a clear justification. How many offices have you visited?
We planned to visit ten, but only four agreed, so we have four.
That worries us, because it's quite a small number.
It is small, but you can make up for it by collecting more responses inside each office. How did you measure the noise?
At first we planned to use a phone app, but it wasn't accurate, so we borrowed a proper sound meter from the physics department.
Sensible. And the questionnaire?
We got eighty-six replies. The problem is that many people left the last section blank. That's the part with the open questions about what they would change.
People often skip open questions when they are busy. You could ask a few of them those questions face to face instead.
That's a good idea. As for the results, the surprising thing was that the loudest office wasn't the one where people complained most.
Yes. In the quietest office, a sudden phone ringing really bothered people, while in the loudest one the steady background noise didn't.
Interesting. That suggests it's the type of noise that matters, rather than the volume. And what did workers say they would prefer?
Most of them didn't want to go back to private rooms. They wanted quiet zones inside the open space.
Right. Now, how will you present all this?
We thought of a poster, but we're wondering about a short report with graphs.

A report would suit this module better, but add a one-page summary at the start. I'd also suggest adding a comparison with the official guidance on safe sound levels, so readers can see how loud is too loud.
Good idea. When do you need the first draft? Is it the twentieth?
No, the twentieth is when the seminars finish. Send me the draft by the twelfth, and the final version is due on the thirtieth.

items.q: Why did the students choose this topic?
options: Noise levels in offices are rising quickly.
Their tutor suggested it to them.
Few studies had asked workers about their feelings.
items.vi: Ít nghiên cứu hỏi người lao động cảm thấy thế nào, đó là khoảng trống.

items.q: What is the students' concern about their research?
options: Some offices refused to answer questions.
Only a small number of offices took part.
The offices were too far away.
items.vi: Chỉ có 4 trong 10 văn phòng đồng ý tham gia.

items.q: How many offices did they visit?
items.vi: Họ dự định thăm 10 văn phòng nhưng chỉ có 4 nơi đồng ý.

items.q: The tutor suggests making up for the small number of offices by
options: collecting more responses in each office
items.vi: Gia sư gợi ý thu thêm phản hồi trong mỗi văn phòng.

items.q: How did the students measure the noise?
options: with a sound meter borrowed from a department
items.vi: Ứng dụng điện thoại không chính xác nên họ mượn máy đo âm thanh.

items.q: What was the problem with the questionnaire?
options: It was too long for most workers.
Many people did not complete the final section.
items.vi: Nhiều người bỏ trống phần cuối gồm các câu hỏi mở.

items.q: What did the tutor suggest about the open questions?
options: Ask some people them in person.
items.vi: Gia sư đề nghị hỏi trực tiếp một số người.

items.q: What surprised the students about their results?
options: Most workers did not notice the noise.
The loudest office had the fewest complaints.
items.vi: Văn phòng ồn nhất lại không phải nơi bị phàn nàn nhiều nhất.

items.q: What did most workers say they preferred?
options: quiet zones inside the open space
items.vi: Hầu hết muốn có khu yên tĩnh trong không gian mở.

items.q: When is the first draft due?
items.vi: Bản nháp nộp ngày 12, bản cuối ngày 30, ngày 20 là hết các buổi seminar.

audio.t: Today I'd like to look at the history of glass, a material so common that we rarely stop to think about where it came from.

Let's begin with nature. Some glass forms naturally when volcanoes throw out hot rock that cools very quickly. This natural glass is called obsidian, and early people used it to make knives and arrow points because it can be made extremely sharp.

Making glass on purpose came later. The main ingredient is sand, but sand alone needs a very high temperature to melt. Craftspeople found that adding soda lowers the melting temperature, and a little lime makes the finished glass stronger.

The earliest man-made glass objects, from about three and a half thousand years ago, were not windows or bottles. They were small beads, which were worn as jewelry. Glass bowls and bottles followed some time afterwards, but they were made by wrapping glass around a core of clay, and that was slow work.

A big change came around fifty BC, when glassblowing was invented. Craftspeople blew air through a tube into a lump of hot glass, and this made hollow objects quickly and cheaply. The new technique appeared in the region that is now Syria, and it spread across the Roman world.

Now let's jump ahead to the Middle Ages. In 1291 the glassmakers of Venice were ordered to move their workshops to the nearby island of Murano. The reason was safety. The furnaces burned all day, and the authorities feared that a fire would destroy the city, which was full of wooden buildings. The move had a useful side effect, because it helped the makers keep their techniques secret.
In the seventeenth century, glassmakers in England discovered that adding lead produced glass that was clear, heavy and brilliant. This is the origin of what we call crystal.

Finally, the modern period. In the nineteen fifties a new process allowed large flat sheets to be made. Molten glass is poured onto a bath of melted tin, where it spreads out and floats, and the result is perfectly smooth window glass. And today, glass has an important role in communication, because the thin glass threads inside fiber optic cables carry internet signals around the world. That brings me to the end of this lecture.

items.text: Natural volcanic glass is called ＿
items.vi: Thủy tinh núi lửa tự nhiên gọi là obsidian, dùng làm dao và mũi tên.

items.text:
A
For most of the twentieth century, city planners treated parks as a pleasant extra. Land in a city is expensive, and a patch of grass that produced neither rent nor taxes was easy to build over. Over the past thirty years, this view has changed sharply. Researchers in many countries have found that green spaces do real work for a city, and that the work can be measured.

B
The best-known benefit is cooling. Streets, parking lots and roofs soak up heat during the day and release it slowly at night, so the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. Trees reduce this effect in two ways. Their leaves cast shade, and they release water vapor that cools the surrounding air. A study in the northern city of Halden found that streets lined with mature trees were, on average, four degrees cooler on summer afternoons than streets without them. As summers become hotter, such a difference can decide whether an elderly resident stays comfortable or ends up in the hospital.

C
Green spaces also appear to affect health. Residents who live within a ten-minute walk of a park tend to exercise more often than those who live farther away. Some doctors in Halden have begun to prescribe regular walks in the park to patients with mild anxiety. However, researchers warn that the size of the effect is easy to exaggerate. People who choose to live near parks are often wealthier and healthier to begin with, so it is difficult to prove that the park itself is the cause of their good health.

D
Parks help in less obvious ways too. When heavy rain falls on concrete, the water runs quickly into the drains, and older drainage systems can overflow and flood the streets. Soil and plants, by contrast, absorb a large share of the rain and release it slowly. Some cities have therefore built rain gardens, which are shallow planted areas designed to hold water during storms. Small habitats of this kind also support wildlife. A survey of rooftop gardens in Halden recorded more than ninety species of insects in a single summer, including several that had not been seen in the city for decades.

E
Creating green space is not simple. Land in the center is costly, so many cities look for creative solutions, such as green roofs, planted walls and pocket parks built on empty lots no bigger than a tennis court. There is also a problem of fairness. In many cities the greenest neighborhoods are the richest. In Halden, a survey showed that the districts with the highest incomes had three times as much park area per person as the poorest districts. Worse, when a new park is built in a poor area, property prices nearby may rise, and the families the park was meant to serve can no longer afford to live there. Some experts call this process green gentrification.

F
Designers now try to involve residents from the very start. In the Brook Street project, planners held a series of meetings with local people before drawing any plans. Residents asked for a playground, a vegetable garden and benches in the shade, and they were also invited to help look after the finished site. Three years later, the park is busy and well cared for, and the number of complaints about damage is lower than in the city's older parks. Experts agree that a park succeeds when people feel that it belongs to them. The future of urban green space may depend less on how much land is set aside than on who is invited to shape it.

items.text:
A
Spoken language is as old as our species, but writing is surprisingly young. For almost all of human history, knowledge was stored in memory and passed on by speech. The first writing appeared only about five thousand years ago, and historians believe it was invented independently in at least three places: Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica. Each invention solved a different local problem, yet all of them began by recording things that people needed to remember.

B
In Mesopotamia, writing began as bookkeeping. Before 3200 BC, traders used small clay tokens to record goods such as sheep and grain. Eventually, someone pressed the shapes of the tokens into a soft clay tablet instead of storing them, and later drew simple pictures of the goods. Over the centuries these pictures turned into wedge-shaped marks made with a cut reed, a style we now call cuneiform. The earliest tablets are not stories or poems. They are lists of goods, payments and workers, and literature appeared much later.

C
Writing systems differ in what a single sign stands for. In a logographic system, such as Chinese, each character represents a word or a meaningful part of a word. Learners must memorize thousands of characters, but there is a great advantage. People who speak very different dialects can read the same text, because the characters carry meaning rather than sound. In a syllabary, such as the Japanese kana, each sign stands for a syllable, so about fifty signs are enough to write every sound of the language. In an alphabet, each sign stands for a single sound, either a consonant or a vowel.

D
The first alphabet is usually credited to people who lived on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean around 1050 BC. It had only twenty-two signs, and all of them were consonants. Greek traders borrowed these signs and made a crucial change: they used some of them to write vowels. The Greek alphabet in turn gave rise to the Latin and Cyrillic scripts. Arabic and Hebrew developed along different lines. Both are still written mainly with consonants, and the reader supplies the vowels from the context.

E
Materials have shaped writing as much as ideas have. Clay was cheap and lasted for thousands of years, but tablets were heavy and impossible to carry in large numbers. Egyptians made papyrus from river reeds, which was light but fragile in damp climates. Parchment, made from animal skin, lasted far longer, yet it was very expensive, because a single large book could require the skins of a whole flock of sheep. Paper, invented in China around AD 105, was cheap and light. When the knowledge of how to make it spread westward, learning no longer depended on a few rich libraries.

F
Not every script evolved slowly. Hangul, the Korean alphabet, was created on purpose in 1443 by scholars working for a king who wanted ordinary people to be able to read. The shapes of its letters copy the position of the mouth and tongue when each sound is made, which makes the system unusually easy to learn. Today keyboards and phones are changing writing once more. Some people worry that handwriting is disappearing, and symbols such as emoji have started to add feeling to short messages. Yet the basic idea behind all these changes is the same as it was in the first clay tablets: marks on a surface can capture what people say and think, and carry it across time and distance.

items.text:
A
A colony of honeybees can contain fifty thousand workers, yet no bee is in charge. There is no leader who gives orders, and the queen's job is to lay eggs, not to make decisions. Even so, the colony finds flowers several kilometers away, sends the right number of workers to each patch and shifts them when the flowers fade. For a long time, no one understood how such coordination was possible. The answer began to emerge in the 1940s, when a zoologist working in Austria noticed that bees returning to the hive sometimes behaved in a strange, repeated pattern.

B
The pattern is now known as the waggle dance. A forager that has found a rich source of food returns to the hive and performs the dance on the vertical surface of the honeycomb, in complete darkness. She walks in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side. This is the waggle run. Then she circles back to her starting point and repeats the run. Other bees crowd around her and follow her movements, touching her with their antennae, because in the dark they cannot watch the dance with their eyes.

C
The dance contains two pieces of information. The first is direction. The angle between the waggle run and the vertical line corresponds to the angle between the food and the sun. If the run points straight up, the food lies in the direction of the sun. If it points 40 degrees to the left of vertical, the bees must fly 40 degrees to the left of the sun. The second is distance. The longer the waggle run lasts, the farther away the food is, and each extra second of waggling roughly means another kilometer, although the exact figure varies between species. Remarkably, the sun moves across the sky while a dancer is still performing, and she adjusts the angle of her dance to correct for it.

D
Dancing is not the only way bees communicate. When food is very close, usually within about fifty meters, a forager performs a simpler round dance, which gives no direction at all, because the other bees can find the flowers by their scent. The dancer carries the smell of the flowers on her body and may share a sample of nectar, so her followers know what to look for. A bee can also tell how good a food source is, because the richer the nectar, the more enthusiastic the dance. Another signal, the tremble dance, is performed by foragers that have been waiting a long time for a receiver bee to take their nectar. It encourages more bees to work inside the hive. A fourth signal is a short head-butt known as the stop signal. Bees that have been attacked at a feeding site give it to dancers, and it reduces the number of recruits sent there.

E
Many scientists doubted these claims at first. In the 1990s, researchers built a small robot bee with a wax-covered body that could imitate the dance. When it performed the correct movements, real bees flew to the feeder it was advertising, although fewer of them arrived than when a live bee did the dancing. Radar tracking of bees leaving the hive has since confirmed that many fly to exactly the places the dancers described. There are differences between species too. The dances of Asian honeybees differ in rhythm from those of European honeybees, and a giant honeybee dances in the open on a sheet of comb, where the dance points directly at the target.

F
Bees also use dancing to make one of the most important decisions in their lives, choosing a new home. When a colony outgrows its nest, scout bees search the area and return to dance for the sites they have found. Better sites get livelier dances, and so they attract more followers. Gradually, scouts change their minds and support the most popular site, and when enough of them are dancing for the same place, the whole swarm takes off together. No single bee has seen all the options, and yet the group nearly always makes a sound choice. Engineers are now studying this process in the hope of designing computer networks and robot swarms that can make good decisions without a central controller.

items.text:
The table shows the number of visitors (in thousands) to four museums in the city of Port Ellery in 2010, 2015 and 2020.

Science Museum: 420 (2010), 465 (2015), 510 (2020)
History Museum: 380 (2010), 350 (2015), 300 (2020)
Art Gallery: 250 (2010), 310 (2015), 420 (2020)
Maritime Museum: 120 (2010), 140 (2015), 95 (2020)

Note: the Maritime Museum was closed for four months in 2020 for building repairs.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares the number of visitors to four museums in Port Ellery in 2010, 2015 and 2020. Overall, the Science Museum and the Art Gallery attracted more visitors over the period, while the History Museum became less popular.

The Science Museum was the most visited museum in every year. Its visitors rose steadily from 420,000 in 2010 to 465,000 in 2015 and finally to 510,000 in 2020, an increase of 90,000. The Art Gallery showed the most dramatic growth. It began as the second least popular museum with 250,000 visitors, but this number climbed to 310,000 in 2015 and then jumped to 420,000 in 2020, which almost matched the figure for the Science Museum in 2010.

In contrast, the History Museum lost visitors in both periods. Its figure fell from 380,000 to 350,000 and then to 300,000, so that by 2020 it had slipped from second place to third place. The Maritime Museum had the smallest numbers throughout. Visitors increased slightly from 120,000 to 140,000 between 2010 and 2015, but fell to 95,000 in 2020. This fall is probably explained by the fact that the museum was closed for four months for repairs.

In summary, the Art Gallery and the Science Museum grew fastest, and the History Museum declined steadily.

items.q:
Some people believe that schools should spend more time teaching practical skills, such as cooking and basic repairs, while others think that academic subjects are more important.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
items.sample:
People disagree about what schools should teach. Some think that practical skills such as cooking and simple repairs deserve more lessons, while others believe that academic subjects like mathematics and science should come first. In my opinion, both are important, but schools should keep a careful balance.

Those who support practical lessons have a strong argument. Most young people will one day have to live on their own, and they will need to prepare healthy meals, manage money and fix small problems at home. A student who has never cooked may depend on expensive fast food, which is bad for both health and savings. Practical lessons are also often more enjoyable, and students who find traditional classes difficult can discover that they are good at something. This may increase their confidence and their interest in school.

On the other hand, academic subjects give students knowledge and thinking skills that they cannot easily learn elsewhere. Mathematics teaches logical reasoning, science explains how the world works, and languages and history help young people to understand other cultures. These subjects are also required for most universities and many careers. If schools reduced the time spent on them, students from poorer families, who depend on school for their education, would suffer most. Parents can teach a child to cook at home, but they cannot always teach chemistry.

For this reason, I believe that the best solution is not to choose one side but to combine the two. For example, a cooking class can include mathematics when students measure ingredients and change a recipe for more people, and a repair workshop can include basic physics. Short practical courses once a week would not take much time away from academic lessons.

In conclusion, although academic subjects must remain the core of the curriculum, schools should also teach practical skills, because together they prepare students better for adult life.

parts.instr: Part 2: Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2: nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong một đến hai phút.

items.q: Describe a piece of music that is special to you. You should say: what the music is, when you first heard it, why you like it, and how you feel when you listen to it.
items.sample: I would like to talk about a piece of piano music that is very special to me. It is a slow, gentle song called Evening Rain, and it was written by a composer from a small country town. I first heard it about four years ago, when I was studying for an important exam. My older cousin was practicing it on our piano at home, and I stopped what I was doing just to listen. I remember that it was raining outside, and the sound of the piano seemed to match the weather perfectly. After that, I asked my cousin to teach me, and I now play a simple version myself. I like this piece because the melody is easy to remember, but it also sounds sad and hopeful at the same time. It reminds me of that period of my life, when I worked hard and had a lot of support from my family. When I listen to it, I feel calm and relaxed, and my worries seem smaller. Whenever I feel stressed, I put on the recording, close my eyes and just breathe slowly. For me, this music is like a good friend who always understands how I feel.
items.vi: Part 2: mô tả bản nhạc đặc biệt, trả lời đủ bốn ý gợi ý trong thẻ.

parts.instr: Part 3: Discuss more abstract questions related to the Part 2 topic.

items.q: Why do you think music is important in people's lives?
items.sample: I think music is important because it helps people express their emotions when words are not enough. It can also bring people together, for example at festivals or family parties. For many people, music is a way to relax after a long day and to remember special moments in their lives.
items.vi: Part 3: thảo luận trừu tượng về vai trò của âm nhạc.

items.q: Do you think young people today listen to different music from their parents? Why?
items.sample: Yes, I think young people often listen to different music, mainly because of technology. They can find songs from any country on their phones, so their taste is wider than their parents' taste used to be. However, some songs from the past are still popular, so the difference is not always big.
items.vi: Part 3: so sánh thị hiếu âm nhạc giữa các thế hệ.

items.q: Should schools make music lessons compulsory for all students?
items.sample: I think schools should offer music lessons to everyone, because they develop creativity and teach students to work as a team. However, I do not think the lessons should be compulsory for the whole school life. Students should be able to choose an instrument or a choir, so that they enjoy it and learn more.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the opening evening of the Riverside Tool Library. My name is Dana Moreno and I coordinate the project.

The idea began three years ago, when a street survey showed that most households owned a drill that they used only once or twice a year. Neighbors realized that it made more sense to share than to buy.
The library started in a garage, but last spring it moved to the old post office on Mill Lane, which gives us three times as much space.
We now have over four hundred items, from ladders and saws to sewing machines and garden equipment. The most popular item by far is the carpet cleaner, which is borrowed almost every weekend.
To borrow, you need to become a member. Membership is free for students and retired people, and costs twelve dollars a year for everyone else.

Members can keep an item for one week. If you need it for longer, you can renew it once, as long as nobody else has reserved it. We don't fine people for late returns. Instead, we ask them to give one hour of volunteer time.

Speaking of volunteers, we always need more. Some help to repair tools on Thursday evenings, and others run the training sessions, but the job we most need help with at the moment is updating our website and booking system.
For safety, anyone borrowing a power tool for the first time has to attend a short training session. These are held on the first Saturday of every month and take about forty minutes.
We are open on Tuesday and Thursday evenings and on Saturday mornings. We'd like to open on Sundays too, but we need a few more volunteers before we can do that.

Finally, next month we are starting a project to teach teenagers basic woodworking skills, with the help of the local college. If you know a young person who might be interested, please speak to me after this talk.

options: People did not know where to buy tools.

A local shop was charging too much for tools.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. You wanted to talk about your presentation on the history of the bicycle.
Yes, Dr Fenwick. We've chosen the period from 1860 to 1900, but we're not sure how to organize it.
What are you thinking of?
I thought we could go year by year, but Priya thinks that would be boring.
It would, because some years have no important changes. I'd prefer to group it around three technical problems: the size of the wheel, the brakes and the tires.
I like that. It gives you a clear structure. But remember that you only have twenty minutes, so don't try to cover everything.
We have lots of photographs from the museum archive. Should we put them all on slides?
Not all of them. Too many images distract the audience. Choose one strong image for each main point and keep the text on each slide to a minimum.
What about the high-wheeler bicycle? It's famous, but we found that it was used by only a small group of wealthy young men.
That's an interesting point. Many people think it was the typical bicycle of the period, so you could challenge that idea.
We also found a letter from a woman in 1890 who describes her first ride. It might make a good introduction.
Excellent. Personal accounts bring history to life. But you must check that it is genuine. Where did you find it?
In a collection of local diaries, but the date is hard to read.
Then ask the archivist to confirm it before you use it.
Should we include a section on how bicycles changed women's lives?
Yes, but be careful. Some writers say that it was the main reason women gained more freedom, but there were many other factors. Present it as one influence among several.
And for the sources, do we need a separate list?
Yes, put it on the final slide. Also hand in a written outline one week before the presentation, which is on the 23rd.
That's fine. We'd like to practice on Monday. Could you sit in?
I'm afraid I'm at a conference on Monday, but I could come on Wednesday afternoon.

Some years had no important changes.

audio.t: Today I'd like to look at the science of earthquakes and at how we try to reduce their effects.

The Earth's outer layer is divided into huge pieces called tectonic plates. These move very slowly, usually only a few centimeters a year, which is about the same speed at which your fingernails grow.
Most earthquakes happen along the edges of the plates, where they push against each other. The pressure builds up for decades, until the rock suddenly breaks.
The point underground where the break begins is called the focus. The point on the surface directly above it is called the epicenter.
The size of an earthquake is measured on a scale from one to ten. Each step up the scale means that about thirty-two times more energy is released.

Scientists cannot predict exactly when an earthquake will happen. What they can do is build early warning systems, which detect the first, weaker waves and send an alert before the stronger shaking arrives.
The warning time is short, from a few seconds up to sixty seconds, but it is enough to stop trains and switch off gas supplies.
Building design matters as well. In Japan, many tall buildings stand on rubber pads, which absorb a lot of the movement.
Simple habits help too. In schools in many countries, children practice 'drop, cover and hold on', which means getting down under a strong table.
It is worth remembering that much of the damage is not caused by the shaking itself, but by fires and landslides afterwards.
That's all for today. For next week, please read chapter seven, which deals with volcanoes.

parts.instr: Questions 1-13. Read the passage and answer the questions.
parts.instrVi: Câu 1-13. Đọc đoạn văn và trả lời các câu hỏi.

items.text:
A
Wind turbines and solar panels now produce a large share of the world's electricity, but they have an obvious weakness: nature does not follow a timetable. The sun sets just when families return home and switch on their lights, and the wind may blow hardest in the middle of the night, when demand is low. Without a way to keep the surplus for later, power stations burning gas or coal must stay ready to fill the gaps. For this reason, many engineers believe that storage, rather than generation, is now the key challenge of the clean energy transition.

B
The oldest and most widespread solution is pumped hydro storage. When electricity is plentiful, pumps lift water from a lower reservoir to a higher one. When demand rises, the water runs back down through turbines and produces power within minutes. A well-built plant can return around three quarters of the energy it consumes and can operate for more than fifty years. Its great limitation is geography. It needs two large bodies of water at different heights, and suitable valleys are scarce, expensive to flood and often opposed by local residents. The Karlsbrook plant in the northern mountains, for instance, took twelve years to plan and nine to build.

C
In recent years, the lithium-ion battery has become the most talked-about alternative. These are the same type of battery found in phones and electric cars, and mass production has pushed their price down dramatically over the past decade. A battery farm can be built in a few months, almost anywhere, and can react to changes in demand in a fraction of a second. However, most installations can supply electricity for only two to four hours. That is enough to cover an evening peak but not a week of calm, cloudy weather. Concerns also remain about the mining of materials such as lithium and cobalt, and about what will happen to millions of worn-out batteries.

D
Because of these limits, researchers are exploring a range of other technologies. Flow batteries store energy in tanks of liquid; to hold more energy, the operator simply builds a larger tank, and the liquid can be used for twenty years without losing capacity. Compressed air systems pump air into underground caves and release it to spin a turbine. In some places, engineers heat containers of molten salt or even sand to very high temperatures, and the stored heat is later turned into steam. Perhaps the most ambitious idea is hydrogen: surplus electricity splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, and the hydrogen can be kept for months in tanks or old gas fields. The process wastes more than half of the energy, however, and the necessary equipment remains costly.

E
Storage is not only a matter for large companies. In a growing number of countries, households with rooftop panels are installing small batteries in their garages, which allows them to use their own midday power in the evening. Some energy companies link thousands of these batteries through software, creating a 'virtual power plant' that can supply the grid at times of stress. Electric cars could play a similar role. A typical car spends more than ninety percent of its life parked, so its battery could feed power back into the grid when needed, provided that owners are paid fairly and that frequent charging does not shorten the battery's life, a point which researchers still debate.

F
Experts increasingly agree that there will be no single winner. Batteries are likely to handle the daily ups and downs, while pumped hydro, heat and hydrogen deal with longer periods. Governments can speed up progress by changing rules that were written for coal and gas plants and that fail to reward storage for the stability it provides. A country that wants to depend mainly on wind and sun will need a mixture of technologies, and it will need to start building them well before the last fossil fuel plant closes.

parts.instr: Questions 14-26. Read the passage and answer the questions.
parts.instrVi: Câu 14-26. Đọc đoạn văn và trả lời các câu hỏi.

items.text:
A
Long before a baby says a first word, the learning has begun. Newborns prefer the sound of their mother's voice, which they heard in the womb, and in the first months they can tell apart the sounds of every language in the world. A baby in Tokyo can hear the difference between 'r' and 'l', even though many adult speakers of Japanese find it hard. By the age of ten to twelve months, however, babies have become specialists. They stop noticing differences that do not matter in their own language and become more skilled at the ones that do.

B
At about six months, babies begin to babble, producing repeated syllables such as 'ba-ba-ba' or 'ma-ma-ma'. Babbling was once thought to be simply a matter of exercising the mouth, but studies of deaf babies raised by deaf parents tell a different story. These infants babble with their hands, repeating small movements that follow the patterns of sign language. It seems that babbling is the brain's way of practicing the rhythm of language, whatever form that language takes.

C
First words usually appear around the first birthday, and for several months children add them slowly, perhaps one or two a week. Then, at around eighteen months, many go through a 'vocabulary spurt', learning several new words each day. Researchers call one mechanism fast mapping: a child hears an unfamiliar word while looking at an unfamiliar object and quickly guesses that the two belong together. Soon afterwards, children begin to join words into short sentences such as 'more juice' or 'Daddy gone'. These early sentences leave out small words, yet the order of the words is almost always correct.

D
What role do adults play? For decades, many people believed that the number of words a child hears was the main factor. A more recent study by researchers at Marlowe University, involving 146 families, suggests that the quality of interaction matters more. Children whose parents regularly took turns in 'conversations' with them, even when the baby could only answer with sounds and smiles, scored higher on language tests at age four than children who simply heard more speech. Many parents instinctively speak to babies in a slow, high-pitched voice with exaggerated vowels. This 'child-directed speech' appears to help infants notice the boundaries between words.

E
Is there an age after which learning a language becomes much harder? Many linguists support the idea of a 'critical period', ending somewhere around puberty. Evidence comes from rare cases of children who grew up without hearing any language and who later learned to speak only with great difficulty. Yet the picture is not simple. Adults can acquire a large vocabulary and complex grammar, and may even learn faster than children in the first months of a course; what they rarely achieve is a native accent. Children raised with two languages usually pass the same milestones as other children, although each language may develop a little more slowly at first. By school age, they are typically able to switch between their languages with ease.

F
Technology has added a new question. Parents often hope that educational videos will teach their toddlers new words. Experiments suggest that children under two learn far fewer words from a screen than from a person in the same room, even when the content is identical. The difference seems to lie in the responses: a live partner points, smiles and reacts to what the child says, whereas a screen cannot. This does not mean that all screen time is harmful, but it reminds us that language is, above all, a social skill.

items.q: Newborn babies are able to distinguish between the sounds of many different languages.
items.vi: Đoạn A: trong những tháng đầu trẻ phân biệt được âm của mọi ngôn ngữ trên thế giới.

items.q: Babies of twelve months hear more sound differences than younger babies.
items.vi: Đoạn A: đến 10-12 tháng trẻ ngừng nhận ra những khác biệt không quan trọng trong tiếng mẹ đẻ.

items.q: Deaf babies who have hearing parents also babble with their hands.
items.vi: Bài chỉ nói về trẻ điếc có cha mẹ điếc, không nói về cha mẹ nghe được.

items.vi: Đoạn D: chất lượng tương tác quan trọng hơn số lượng lời nói.

items.q: Adults can sometimes make faster progress than children at the start of a language course.
items.vi: Đoạn E: người lớn có thể học nhanh hơn trẻ em trong vài tháng đầu.

items.q: What do studies of deaf babies suggest about babbling?

It begins later than in hearing babies.
It is a way for the brain to practice the rhythm of language.
It only exercises the muscles of the mouth.
items.vi: Đoạn B: bập bẹ là cách não luyện nhịp điệu ngôn ngữ, dù bằng tay hay bằng miệng.

items.q: What does the term 'fast mapping' describe?
options: Learning to read at an early age
Linking a new word with a new object very quickly
items.vi: Đoạn C: trẻ nghe từ lạ khi nhìn vật lạ và nhanh chóng đoán hai thứ đi cùng nhau.

options: Taking turns in conversation helps more than hearing many words.
Parents should talk to babies as much as possible.
Babies prefer to hear only their mother's voice.
Language tests at age four are not reliable.
items.vi: Đoạn D: những đứa trẻ được trò chuyện qua lại đạt điểm cao hơn.

options: Videos teach different words from people.
Children learn less from screens because screens do not respond.
Screens should be banned for young children.
Toddlers learn best from educational videos.
items.vi: Đoạn F: người thật phản hồi còn màn hình thì không, nên trẻ học được ít từ hơn.

items.vi: Đoạn C: trẻ ghép từ thành câu ngắn như 'more juice'.

items.vi: Đoạn D: cha mẹ nói chậm, giọng cao, nguyên âm kéo dài (child-directed speech).

items.q: Which paragraph discusses a possible age limit for language learning?
items.vi: Đoạn E bàn về 'giai đoạn then chốt' (critical period).

items.vi: Đoạn A: đến 10-12 tháng trẻ thôi chú ý những khác biệt không quan trọng.

parts.instr: Questions 27-40. Read the passage and answer the questions.
parts.instrVi: Câu 27-40. Đọc đoạn văn và trả lời các câu hỏi.

items.text:
A
The name 'Silk Road' suggests a single highway stretching from China to the Mediterranean, but the reality was very different. It was a web of overland and sea routes that developed gradually over more than a thousand years. Few traders ever traveled the whole distance. Instead, goods passed through many hands, each merchant buying in one town and selling in the next at a higher price. The term itself is modern: it was invented by a German geographer in the nineteenth century, long after the great caravans had disappeared.

B
Silk was only one of many products. Chinese paper and porcelain traveled west, while glass, gold and silver, wool and fine horses traveled east. Spices such as pepper and cinnamon, which grew in southern Asia, were so valuable in Mediterranean cities that they were sometimes weighed against silver. Some goods were surprising. Archaeologists have found tiny pieces of lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone mined only in the mountains of northern Afghanistan, in tombs thousands of kilometers away, which shows how far a luxury item could be carried.

C
Crossing deserts and mountains demanded both skill and organization. The two-humped Bactrian camel, which could carry about two hundred kilograms and survive for days with little water, was the animal of choice. Along the main routes, rulers and wealthy merchants built caravanserais, large inns where travelers could rest, store their goods and exchange news. These buildings, often spaced about a day's journey apart, were protected by walls and guards. Many offered food and water for animals at no cost, because a ruler who kept his roads safe collected taxes from the profitable trade.

D
Alongside the land routes grew a sea network that linked the east coast of Africa, Arabia, India and Southeast Asia. Sailors learned to use the monsoon winds, which blow from the southwest in summer and from the northeast in winter. A ship could therefore leave India with the summer wind, trade on the African coast and return with the winter wind within a single year. Sea transport could carry far more cargo than a camel, and by the first centuries of the modern era, many bulky goods, such as pottery and timber, were moving by ship rather than by caravan.

E
The routes carried more than goods. Paper-making, which began in China, reached the Islamic world by the eighth century and then Europe, where it eventually made books much cheaper. Our modern numbers, developed in India, spread west along the same paths, as did new crops such as oranges, rice and sugar cane. Music, stories and styles of art mixed in the busy cities along the way. Disease traveled too. Historians believe that the plague of the fourteenth century followed trade routes, killing a large part of the population in the cities that had grown rich from commerce.

F
By the fifteenth century, the overland routes were declining. The collapse of the large empire that had kept the roads safe made travel more dangerous and taxes higher. Meanwhile, European sailors, looking for a way to reach Asian markets without paying the many middlemen, developed ships that could cross open oceans. The sea route around Africa was slower than the monsoon trade, but it avoided the long chain of tolls. Even so, the old routes never disappeared completely. Some towns that began as stopping points are still important cities today, and archaeologists continue to discover new evidence of this ancient network.

items.q: Most traders traveled the whole length of the Silk Road.
items.vi: Đoạn A: rất ít thương nhân đi hết toàn bộ quãng đường, hàng hóa được chuyển qua nhiều tay.

items.q: The name 'Silk Road' was first used by a geographer from Germany.
items.vi: Đoạn A: thuật ngữ này do một nhà địa lý người Đức đặt ra vào thế kỷ 19.

items.q: Lapis lazuli was worth more than silver in Mediterranean cities.
items.vi: Bài chỉ nói gia vị được cân bằng bạc, không so sánh giá trị của lapis lazuli.

items.vi: Đoạn C: nhiều nhà trọ cung cấp thức ăn và nước cho súc vật miễn phí.

items.q: Ships on the monsoon route were larger than European ocean ships.
items.vi: Bài không so sánh kích cỡ tàu của hai tuyến này.

items.q: Why did goods usually pass through many hands?
options: Silk could only be sold by local traders.
Caravans were too small to travel far.
Few merchants traveled the entire route.
items.vi: Đoạn A: thương nhân mua ở thị trấn này rồi bán lại ở thị trấn kế tiếp.

items.q: Why was the Bactrian camel preferred?
options: It could carry heavy loads and manage with little water.
It was cheap to buy and feed.
It could cross the sea on ships.
It could travel faster than a horse.
items.vi: Đoạn C: lạc đà hai bướu chở khoảng 200 kg và chịu khát nhiều ngày.

options: Safe roads brought them tax income from trade.
They wanted to attract foreign scholars.
items.vi: Đoạn C: vua chúa giữ đường an toàn để thu thuế từ việc buôn bán sinh lợi.

options: It was too dangerous for valuable goods.
It was used for bulky goods such as pottery and timber.
It was slower than caravans in every case.
It was only used between India and China.
items.vi: Đoạn D: nhiều hàng cồng kềnh như đồ gốm, gỗ được chở bằng tàu thay vì đoàn lạc đà.

options: followed the routes used by traders.
began in the cities of Europe.
items.vi: Đoạn E: các nhà sử học tin rằng dịch hạch lan theo các tuyến thương mại.

items.vi: Đoạn E: các loại cây trồng mới như cam, lúa gạo, mía lan sang phía tây.

items.q: Which paragraph explains how seasonal winds were used?
items.vi: Đoạn D: thủy thủ tận dụng gió mùa hè và gió mùa đông.

items.q: Which paragraph shows that a luxury item traveled far from its source?
items.vi: Đoạn B: đá lapis lazuli tìm thấy trong các ngôi mộ cách xa hàng nghìn km.

parts.instr: Task 1. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.
parts.instrVi: Bài 1. Bạn nên dành khoảng 20 phút cho bài này.

items.text:
The table shows the number of visitors (in thousands) to the Harbour City Museum in 2005, 2015 and 2025, divided into three groups.

Local adults: 120 in 2005, 135 in 2015, 110 in 2025.
Tourists: 60 in 2005, 140 in 2015, 210 in 2025.
School groups: 45 in 2005, 50 in 2015, 85 in 2025.
Total visitors: 225 in 2005, 325 in 2015, 405 in 2025.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares the number of visitors, in thousands, to the Harbour City Museum in three different years: 2005, 2015 and 2025. Overall, the museum became much more popular over the period, and the main reason was a steady rise in tourists.

In 2005, local adults were the largest group, with 120,000 visits, while tourists accounted for 60,000 and school groups for 45,000. By 2015, the number of local adults had risen slightly to 135,000, but tourist visits more than doubled to 140,000, which made them the biggest group.

The trend continued in 2025. Tourist numbers reached 210,000, which is more than three times the figure in 2005. School groups also grew, particularly between 2015 and 2025, when they went up from 50,000 to 85,000. In contrast, local adults were the only group to decline, falling to 110,000. As a result, the total number of visitors increased from 225,000 in 2005 to 405,000 in 2025, an increase of 80 percent.
items.vi: Bài mô tả bảng số liệu: mở bài nêu nội dung, nêu xu hướng chung (khách du lịch tăng mạnh), so sánh từng nhóm theo từng năm và dùng số liệu cụ thể.

parts.instr: Task 2. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.
parts.instrVi: Bài 2. Bạn nên dành khoảng 40 phút cho bài này.

items.q: Some people think that governments should spend money on preserving old buildings. Others believe that this money would be better spent on new housing, hospitals and roads. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
items.sample:
People disagree about whether public money should be used to protect old buildings or to provide new facilities. In my opinion, both aims are important, but a balance is needed, and basic services should come first.

On the one hand, there are good reasons to preserve old buildings. They are a record of our history, and they show younger generations how people lived and worked in the past. Many historic districts also attract tourists, who spend money in local shops, hotels and restaurants. Once an old building has been demolished, it can never be replaced, so a decision to protect it is a decision for the long term.

On the other hand, the funds of any government are limited, and there are urgent needs. In many cities, families wait years for affordable housing, and hospitals are crowded. New roads and public transport can reduce travel times and make daily life easier for millions of people. It is hard to argue that a museum roof should be repaired before a clinic is built in a poor neighborhood.

However, the two goals do not always compete. Old buildings can be given a new purpose, for example as apartments, schools or community centers. This approach protects the past and meets modern needs at the same time, and it is often cheaper than building from nothing. Governments could also encourage private owners to share the cost of repairs through tax benefits.

In conclusion, I believe that governments should give priority to housing, health and transport, but they should still set aside a reasonable amount to protect the most important historic buildings. With careful planning, a city can respect its heritage and prepare for the future.
items.vi: Bài nghị luận hai quan điểm: nêu lý do ủng hộ bảo tồn, lý do ủng hộ xây mới, rồi đưa ý kiến riêng (cân bằng, ưu tiên dịch vụ cơ bản) và kết luận rõ ràng.

parts.instr: Part 1. Answer the questions about familiar topics.
parts.instrVi: Phần 1. Trả lời các câu hỏi về chủ đề quen thuộc.

items.q: Let's talk about your home. What is your favorite room in your home, and why?
items.sample: My favorite room is the living room because it is the place where my family spends most of the evening. We watch films together, play board games and talk about our day, so the room always feels warm and friendly.
items.vi: Trả lời nêu phòng yêu thích, lý do (because) và một vài chi tiết cụ thể.

items.q: Do you prefer cooking at home or eating in restaurants?
items.sample: I prefer cooking at home, although I sometimes go to restaurants with friends. Cooking is cheaper and healthier, and I enjoy trying new recipes, but restaurants are useful when I am tired or want to celebrate something.
items.vi: Nêu sự lựa chọn (prefer), so sánh hai lựa chọn và đưa lý do.

items.q: How do you usually travel to school or work?
items.sample: I usually go by bus because my school is about six kilometers from my house. The journey takes around thirty minutes, so I often listen to music or read on the way. When the weather is nice, I sometimes ride my bike.
items.vi: Nói về phương tiện thường dùng, thời gian di chuyển và một thói quen khác.

items.q: What do you usually do at the weekend?
items.sample: At the weekend I usually sleep a little later than on school days. In the morning I help my parents with housework, and in the afternoon I meet my friends to play football or go to the park. On Sunday evenings I prepare for the next week.
items.vi: Mô tả hoạt động cuối tuần theo trình tự thời gian.

parts.instr: Part 2. Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2. Nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong một đến hai phút.

items.q: Describe a skill that you learned and that you find useful. You should say: what the skill is; when and how you learned it; who helped you; and explain why this skill is useful to you.
items.sample: I would like to talk about swimming, which is a skill that I learned when I was eight years old. At first I was afraid of the water, and I even refused to put my face under it, but my aunt, who was a swimming teacher, helped me a lot. She took me to the local pool every Saturday morning for about three months. She did not push me too hard. Instead, she taught me to breathe properly and to relax, and she praised every small step that I made. The first time I swam a whole length of the pool without stopping, I felt extremely proud. Since then, I have practiced regularly, and now I can swim for more than an hour. I think swimming is very useful for several reasons. First, it keeps me healthy and strong, because it exercises the whole body. Second, it is a safety skill, because it could save my life or another person's life near water. Finally, it helps me to relax after a stressful week at school. I am very grateful to my aunt for teaching me.
items.vi: Bài nói Part 2: nêu kỹ năng, khi nào và học như thế nào, ai giúp, rồi giải thích lý do hữu ích; dùng thì quá khứ cho kỷ niệm và thì hiện tại cho lợi ích.

parts.instr: Part 3. Discuss the questions about skills and learning.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3. Thảo luận các câu hỏi về kỹ năng và việc học.

items.q: Which skills do you think schools should teach that they do not teach at the moment?
items.sample: I think schools should teach practical skills such as managing money, cooking and basic first aid. At the moment students spend a lot of time on theory, but many leave school without knowing how to make a budget or what to do in an emergency. These skills are important for everyday life, and they would make young people more independent.
items.vi: Nêu quan điểm, đưa ví dụ kỹ năng thực tế và giải thích vì sao quan trọng.

items.q: Do you think it is better to learn a skill from a teacher or to teach yourself?
items.sample: In my view, it depends on the skill. A teacher is better for difficult or dangerous skills, because they can correct your mistakes and explain things clearly. However, teaching yourself is a good way to learn at your own speed, and today there are many videos and websites to help. I think the best way is to combine both, so you get guidance and freedom.
items.vi: So sánh hai cách học, nêu ưu nhược điểm và đưa ra kết luận cân bằng.

items.q: How do you think the skills that people need for work will change in the future?
items.sample: I believe that technology will change most jobs in the future, so people will need to learn new skills throughout their lives. Computer skills will be more important, but so will skills that machines cannot copy easily, such as creativity, teamwork and communication. Workers who are willing to keep learning will have a big advantage.

audio.t: Good morning, Northgate Climbing Centre. How can I help you?
Hi, I'd like to join the centre. Could you tell me about membership?
Of course. First, can I take your name?
It's Daniel Brennick. That's B-R-E-N-N-I-C-K.
Thank you, Daniel. Are you a student?
Yes, I'm studying design at the university.
Then you can have the student pass. It's thirty-eight dollars a month, which is cheaper than the adult pass at forty-five.
That sounds good. Is there a long contract?
No, you can stop at any time. But everyone has to do an induction course before climbing. It lasts two hours.
Can I do it this weekend?
There's a session on Saturday at nine, but it's full. The next one is at ten.
Ten o'clock is fine. Do I need to bring my own shoes?
No, you can hire them. Shoe hire is four dollars a visit, and the chalk is free.
Great. Do you need my address?
Yes, please.
It's 12 Hallam Road. Hallam is H-A-L-L-A-M.
Thank you. And we need an emergency contact, in case of an accident.
My sister. I'll write her number on the form when I arrive.
That's fine. How did you hear about us?
A friend mentioned the centre, but it was a poster in the student union that made me call.
Lovely. Your locker will be number forty-seven. The lockers by the entrance are forty to forty-five, but yours is a little further along.
Thanks very much. See you on Saturday!

audio.t: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming to this information evening about the Millbrook Sunday Market. I'm the market manager, and I'd like to tell you what is new this year.

The market began in 2016 with just eight stalls in the car park behind the sports hall. Last year it grew to sixty stalls, and this spring we have moved to the old railway yard, which has much more space and a roof over half of it.

Our main rule has not changed. Every stall holder must grow, bake or make what they sell, and they must live within thirty miles of the town. That means no goods bought from wholesalers, however cheap they are.

There are three big changes this year. First, we now open at eight instead of nine, because many of you said in our survey that you wanted to shop before the heat of the day. Stall holders will still arrive at seven to set up.

Second, on the first Sunday of every month we will hold a craft day, with workshops for children. Third, we are starting a food scheme. At four o'clock, any unsold vegetables and bread will go to the community kitchen on Mill Street instead of being thrown away.

We still need volunteers. The most urgent need is for people to help with setting up in the morning. We would also like someone to run the information table, but we can manage without that for now. Volunteers receive a coffee and a bag of vegetables to take home.

A word about parking. The railway yard car park is only for stall holders and disabled visitors. Please use the Bridge Street car park, which is free on Sundays and only a five-minute walk. The car park by the station costs three dollars, so I would avoid it.

Finally, if you would like to rent a stall, the price is twenty dollars a day. New businesses pay half price for their first month. Applications are made online through the town council website. We no longer accept paper forms. Thank you, and now I'm happy to take your questions.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your survey project?
Yes, Dr Hale. We're looking at how students travel to the university, and what would make more of them use the bus.
We've written a questionnaire with twenty-five questions, but Priya thinks it might be too long.
I do. When I tried it on my flatmates, they were bored after the first page.
She's right. Once you go above about fifteen questions, people start ticking boxes without thinking. Which questions are essential?
How far they live from campus, and how they usually travel.
Good. I would remove the question about family income. Many people find it too personal and may refuse to answer.
We wanted to ask about income because cost seems important.
Then ask how much they spend each week on travel. That gives you the same information without the awkward question.
Okay. We planned to stand outside the student cafe and ask people as they came out.
I would be careful. You would only reach people who go to the cafe, so your results could be biased. Try several places and times, including early morning.
How many responses do we need?
For a project this size, about a hundred and twenty is reasonable. Three hundred would be too many to analyse before your deadline, and sixty would be too few.
Should we tell people what the survey is for?
Yes. Explain at the start that their answers are anonymous and that taking part is voluntary. You also need to fill in a short ethics form, which I can sign.
For the analysis, we were thinking of using a spreadsheet. Is that good enough?
For percentages and simple charts, a spreadsheet is perfectly adequate. You don't need the statistics software on this project.
And the presentation? We want to show everything we found.
Please don't. Choose the three clearest findings and show one chart for each. Your audience will remember more.
When should we hand in the report?
At the end of the month. But before that, I would like you to try the questionnaire on five or six people this week. It's called a pilot, and it will show you which questions confuse people.
We'll do that on Thursday. Thank you, Dr Hale.

items.q: What problem does Priya mention about the questionnaire?
items.vi: Priya cho rằng bảng hỏi quá dài vì bạn cùng nhà của cô chán sau trang đầu.

items.q: What is the largest number of questions Dr Hale recommends?
items.vi: Trên khoảng 15 câu thì người trả lời bắt đầu đánh dấu bừa; 25 là số câu hiện có.

items.q: Why does Dr Hale suggest removing the question about income?
options: It is not related to the project.
It takes too long to answer.
Many people find it too personal.
items.vi: Thầy cho rằng nhiều người thấy câu hỏi về thu nhập quá riêng tư nên có thể từ chối trả lời.

items.q: What does he suggest asking instead?
options: How much students spend on travel each week
items.vi: Thay vào đó hỏi mỗi tuần sinh viên chi bao nhiêu cho việc đi lại.

items.q: What is the problem with standing outside the student cafe?
options: The university does not allow it.
It would be too cold in the morning.
Only certain kinds of students would be asked.
items.vi: Chỉ gặp những người hay đến quán cà phê nên kết quả bị thiên lệch.

items.q: How many responses does Dr Hale think is reasonable?
items.vi: Khoảng 120 phản hồi là hợp lý; 300 quá nhiều còn 60 quá ít.

items.q: What must participants be told at the start?

items.vi: Phải nói rõ câu trả lời ẩn danh và việc tham gia là tự nguyện.

audio.t: Good afternoon. Today I'm going to talk about glaciers, which are large masses of ice that move slowly over land. Glaciers cover about ten percent of the Earth's land surface, and they hold most of the world's fresh water.

A glacier begins to form when more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, new layers of snow bury the old ones. The weight squeezes out the air, and the snow is gradually compressed into dense ice. In cold, dry regions this can take several centuries.

Once a glacier is about fifty metres thick, it starts to flow under its own weight. The movement is slow, from a few centimetres to several metres a day. In a valley glacier, the ice in the centre moves faster than the ice at the sides, because the sides are slowed by friction with the rocks.
The surface layer is brittle. When the ice is stretched over a bump in the ground, deep cracks open up. These cracks are called crevasses, and they are a serious danger to climbers.

Scientists value glaciers because they keep a record of the past. When snow falls, it traps small bubbles of air. By drilling long cylinders of ice, called ice cores, researchers can analyse these bubbles and learn about the atmosphere and the climate of hundreds of thousands of years ago.
Glaciers are also important for people living downstream. In summer, meltwater flows into rivers and provides water for farming and drinking in the dry months.

Sadly, most glaciers are now shrinking. Measurements in the Alps show that glaciers there have lost about half of their volume since 1900. Today we monitor these changes with satellite images, which can cover remote regions that are too dangerous to visit. In the next lecture, we will look at how glacier retreat affects sea level.

A glacier begins to form when more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, new layers of snow bury the old ones. The weight squeezes out the air, and the snow is gradually compressed into dense ice. In cold, dry regions this can take several centuries.

Once a glacier is about fifty metres thick, it starts to flow under its own weight. The movement is slow, from a few centimetres to several metres a day. In a valley glacier, the ice in the centre moves faster than the ice at the sides, because the sides are slowed by friction with the rocks.
The surface layer is brittle. When the ice is stretched over a bump in the ground, deep cracks open up. These cracks are called crevasses, and they are a serious danger to climbers.

Scientists value glaciers because they keep a record of the past. When snow falls, it traps small bubbles of air. By drilling long cylinders of ice, called ice cores, researchers can analyse these bubbles and learn about the atmosphere and the climate of hundreds of thousands of years ago.
Glaciers are also important for people living downstream. In summer, meltwater flows into rivers and provides water for farming and drinking in the dry months.

Sadly, most glaciers are now shrinking. Measurements in the Alps show that glaciers there have lost about half of their volume since 1900. Today we monitor these changes with satellite images, which can cover remote regions that are too dangerous to visit. In the next lecture, we will look at how glacier retreat affects sea level.

items.text:
A. For centuries, people assumed that sleep was simply a time when the brain switched off to rest. Modern research has shown the opposite. While we sleep, the brain remains highly active, and much of this activity appears to be devoted to handling the memories formed during the day. Scientists now believe that a good night's sleep is as important for learning as the time spent studying itself.

B. Sleep is not a single state. During a typical night, a person moves through several cycles, each lasting about ninety minutes and containing lighter sleep, deep sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. In deep sleep, also called slow-wave sleep, brain cells fire together in slow, regular waves. In REM sleep, brain activity looks similar to that of a waking person, and vivid dreams are most common. Researchers have found that these stages serve different memory functions. Deep sleep seems to help with facts and events, such as vocabulary lists or the details of a journey, while REM sleep is linked to skills and emotional experiences.

C. One of the most widely accepted explanations involves a small structure called the hippocampus, which acts as a temporary store for new information. During the day, the hippocampus records experiences quickly but has limited capacity. In deep sleep, it appears to replay the day's patterns of activity, sending them gradually to the cortex, the outer layer of the brain, where they can be kept for the long term. Experiments with rats support this idea. The same sequence of brain cells that fired as an animal ran through a maze was found to fire again, at higher speed, while the animal slept. Short bursts of activity called sleep spindles are thought to help carry out this transfer, and people who produce more spindles often perform better on memory tests.

D. A well-known study led by the researcher Dr Anna Lindqvist asked two groups of students to learn forty pairs of unrelated words. One group learned the words in the evening and then slept normally. The other learned them in the morning and stayed awake all day. When both groups were tested twelve hours later, the students who had slept remembered about twenty percent more pairs. Even more striking, when the groups were tested again a week later, the gap between them had not closed, which suggests that sleep protects memories over a long period rather than only for a night.

E. Sleep also prepares the brain for learning in advance. A lack of sleep the night before a study session reduces the activity of the hippocampus, making it harder to absorb new information. In one experiment, volunteers who had been kept awake for a whole night were shown a series of pictures, and they later recalled around forty percent fewer of them than rested volunteers. This finding is worrying for students who stay up late before examinations, a habit known as cramming. Researchers suggest that, instead of studying through the night, learners should divide their revision into shorter sessions spread over several days, with a full night's sleep in between.

F. Not all the news concerns long nights. A short nap of twenty to thirty minutes in the afternoon has been shown to improve alertness and, in some studies, to help people retain newly learned material. However, naps of more than an hour may cause a groggy feeling known as sleep inertia. Scientists are cautious about claiming too much. Some laboratories have played quiet sounds linked to a learned task while volunteers were in deep sleep, and have found small improvements in recall, but the effects are modest and the methods are still being tested. For now, the best advice is the simplest: aim for seven to nine hours of sleep each night.

items.q: In the past, many people believed that the brain rested completely during sleep.
items.vi: Đoạn A: người ta từng cho rằng não 'tắt đi' khi ngủ, nên câu này đúng.

items.q: A sleep cycle always lasts exactly ninety minutes.
items.vi: Đoạn B nói mỗi chu kỳ kéo dài khoảng (about) 90 phút, không phải luôn chính xác 90 phút.

items.q: Sleep spindles are more common in young people than in older people.
items.vi: Bài chỉ nói người có nhiều sleep spindles thường làm bài kiểm tra trí nhớ tốt hơn, không nói về tuổi tác.

items.q: Deep sleep seems to be more closely linked to facts than to skills.
items.vi: Đoạn B: giấc ngủ sâu giúp ghi nhớ sự kiện, còn REM liên quan đến kỹ năng.

items.q: In the word-pair study, the difference between the two groups disappeared after a week.
items.vi: Đoạn D: sau một tuần khoảng cách giữa hai nhóm vẫn chưa được thu hẹp.

items.q: Which paragraph describes an experiment on animals?
items.vi: Đoạn C nhắc đến thí nghiệm với chuột đi qua mê cung.

items.q: Which paragraph gives advice on how to organise revision?
items.vi: Đoạn E khuyên chia nhỏ việc ôn tập ra nhiều ngày thay vì thức xuyên đêm.

items.q: Which paragraph explains that sleep has different stages?
items.vi: Đoạn B mô tả các chu kỳ gồm giấc ngủ nông, ngủ sâu và REM.

items.q: Which paragraph mentions a limit to what scientists currently know?
items.vi: Đoạn F nói các nhà khoa học thận trọng, hiệu quả còn nhỏ và phương pháp vẫn đang thử nghiệm.

items.q: What is the main point of paragraph A?
options: The brain is active during sleep and deals with memories.
People today sleep less than people in the past.
Scientists cannot agree on why people sleep.
Studying is less important than sleeping.
items.vi: Đoạn A: não vẫn hoạt động khi ngủ và xử lý các ký ức hình thành trong ngày.

items.q: According to paragraph C, what is the role of the hippocampus?
options: It stops the cortex from replaying the day.
It holds new information briefly before it moves to the cortex.
It controls the speed of sleep waves.
items.vi: Hippocampus là nơi lưu tạm thời, sau đó thông tin được chuyển sang vỏ não để lưu lâu dài.

items.q: Why did the volunteers in the picture experiment recall fewer pictures?
options: They had not revised in advance.
Their hippocampus was less able to take in information.
They were given too little time to look.
items.vi: Đoạn E: thiếu ngủ làm giảm hoạt động của hippocampus nên khó tiếp thu thông tin mới.

items.q: What does the writer say about playing sounds during deep sleep?
options: It has produced small improvements so far.
items.vi: Đoạn F: các âm thanh nhẹ chỉ cải thiện khả năng nhớ một chút, hiệu quả còn khiêm tốn.
