items.text:
A. Tourism is one of the largest industries in the world. By common estimates, travel and tourism accounts for about one tenth of global economic output and supports hundreds of millions of jobs. Economists treat money spent by foreign visitors as a kind of export, because it brings income into a country from outside. Unlike a normal export, however, the customer comes to the product rather than the product going to the customer, and this changes who benefits and who pays.

B. The main economic argument for tourism is the multiplier effect. When a visitor pays for a hotel room, the hotel uses part of that money to pay its cleaners and cooks, buy fish from a local supplier and repair its roof. Those workers and suppliers in turn spend their earnings in nearby shops and cafes, so a single payment passes through the community several times. The size of the multiplier depends on how much of the money stays in the area. Where hotels buy local produce and employ local people, the effect is large. Where they do not, it is small.

C. The problem is known as leakage. In many developing destinations, resorts are owned by foreign companies, and a large share of each payment flows straight back out of the country as profit, imported food and fuel, or fees to overseas booking platforms. One often-quoted study of small island states suggested that in some cases more than half of tourist spending never reached the local economy. On the island of Tavora, for example, a large resort once imported almost all of its fruit and vegetables, even though local farmers could grow them. After the government required hotels to buy at least a third of their produce locally, farm incomes in the nearby villages rose by roughly a quarter within three years.

D. A second weakness is seasonality. Many destinations attract visitors only in a few months of the year, so jobs are short-term and often poorly paid. In the coastal town of Port Veldra, for instance, around seventy percent of annual visitor spending is concentrated between June and August, and many cafes close for the rest of the year. Dependence on one industry also leaves a region exposed to shocks that nobody can control. A storm, a rise in air fares, a change in fashion or a sudden travel ban can remove most of a town's income within weeks.

E. Tourism also imposes costs on people who live in popular places. As demand for short-term holiday rentals grows, landlords may prefer visitors to long-term tenants, pushing up rents and forcing residents out of central districts. Water supplies, roads and waste collection must be built to cope with peak numbers, even though they are used fully for only part of the year. In the city of Calmora, concern about overcrowding led the council to charge day visitors a small entry fee. Revenue from the fee has helped to pay for street cleaning, but surveys suggest that it has done little to reduce the number of people arriving, because the fee is low compared with the total cost of a trip.

F. Most economists therefore conclude that tourism is neither a guaranteed blessing nor an inevitable curse. Its value depends on policy. Governments can encourage visitors to travel outside the peak months, spread them across several regions instead of a few famous sites, and support businesses that are owned by local families. Diversification is equally important. Towns that develop other industries alongside tourism, such as food processing or crafts, are better able to survive a bad year. The most successful destinations, it seems, are those that treat tourism as one part of a wider economy rather than the whole of it.

items.q: Economists treat money spent by foreign tourists as a kind of export.
items.vi: Đoạn A: tiền của du khách nước ngoài được coi là một dạng xuất khẩu vì mang thu nhập từ bên ngoài vào.

items.q: The multiplier effect is the same size in every destination.
items.vi: Đoạn B: quy mô hiệu ứng nhân phụ thuộc vào lượng tiền ở lại địa phương nên không giống nhau.

items.q: Resorts owned by foreign companies make higher profits than locally owned ones.
items.vi: Bài chỉ nói lợi nhuận chảy ra nước ngoài, không so sánh mức lợi nhuận giữa hai loại khu nghỉ dưỡng.

items.q: The entry fee in Calmora has greatly reduced the number of day visitors.
items.vi: Đoạn E: các khảo sát cho thấy khoản phí này hầu như không làm giảm lượng khách.

items.q: Which paragraph explains how one payment can support several local businesses?
items.vi: Đoạn B giải thích một khoản thanh toán đi qua cộng đồng nhiều lần (hiệu ứng nhân).

items.q: Which paragraph gives an example of a policy that helped local farmers?
items.vi: Đoạn C: chính phủ yêu cầu khách sạn mua nông sản địa phương nên thu nhập nông dân tăng.

items.q: Which paragraph describes the risk of relying on a single industry?
items.vi: Đoạn D nói phụ thuộc vào một ngành khiến vùng dễ bị tổn thương trước các cú sốc.

items.q: Which paragraph describes the effect of tourism on housing?
items.vi: Đoạn E: nhà cho thuê ngắn hạn làm tăng giá thuê và đẩy cư dân ra khỏi trung tâm.

items.q: In paragraph A, how is tourism different from an ordinary export?
options: It does not bring income from abroad.
The customer comes to the product.
It is much smaller than other industries.
items.vi: Đoạn A: với du lịch, khách hàng đến với sản phẩm chứ không phải sản phẩm đến với khách hàng.

items.q: What does the word leakage refer to in paragraph C?
options: A fall in the number of visitors
items.vi: Leakage là việc một phần lớn tiền du khách chảy ra khỏi nền kinh tế địa phương.

items.q: What happened on Tavora after hotels were told to buy local produce?
options: Farm incomes in nearby villages rose.
items.vi: Sau quy định mua nông sản địa phương, thu nhập của nông dân tăng khoảng một phần tư.

items.q: According to paragraph D, what is one problem of seasonality?
options: Local people leave town for the summer.
Hotels are too expensive in summer.
Many jobs are short-term and poorly paid.
Visitors prefer to travel in winter.
items.vi: Đoạn D: nhiều công việc ngắn hạn và lương thấp vì khách chỉ đến vài tháng trong năm.

items.q: What is the writer's conclusion in paragraph F?
options: Only small towns can benefit from tourism.
Governments should stop all visitors in summer.
Tourism should be avoided by poor countries.
The value of tourism depends on how it is managed.
items.vi: Đoạn F: du lịch không phải phước lành hay lời nguyền, giá trị của nó phụ thuộc vào chính sách.

parts.instrVi: Đọc đoạn văn và trả lời các câu hỏi.

items.text:
A. The oceans cover about seventy percent of the Earth's surface, yet the deepest parts remain less known than many distant planets. The deep sea is usually defined as the water below about 200 metres, where sunlight begins to fade. Below 1,000 metres there is no light at all, the temperature is close to freezing and the pressure is hundreds of times greater than at the surface. These extreme conditions make exploration technically demanding and very expensive.

B. Early attempts to study the depths relied on simple tools. In the nineteenth century, scientists lowered weighted ropes from ships to measure depth and dragged nets along the bottom to collect animals. Many believed that nothing could live in the dark, cold water far below. This view was overturned when ships brought up living creatures from thousands of metres down. The first crewed dive to the deepest known point, in the Pacific Ocean, took place in 1960 in a heavy steel vessel. It reached almost 11,000 metres, but the crew could stay only about twenty minutes and saw very little. After that, few crewed dives were made for decades.

C. A turning point came in 1977, when a small research submersible exploring a ridge on the floor of the Pacific found hot water streaming from chimney-like structures, later named hydrothermal vents. Around them lived dense communities of giant tube worms, clams and crabs. Without sunlight, these animals depended on bacteria that make food from chemicals such as hydrogen sulphide, a process called chemosynthesis. The discovery showed that life does not always depend on the sun, and it changed scientists' thinking about where life might exist, including on other worlds.

D. Today most exploration is carried out by machines. Remotely operated vehicles, or ROVs, are connected to a ship by a cable that carries power and sends back video, and a pilot on deck controls their mechanical arms to collect samples. Autonomous underwater vehicles, or AUVs, carry no cable. They follow a programmed route and return with maps and measurements. AUVs can cover large areas at low cost, but they cannot easily react to something unexpected, while ROVs allow scientists to examine a surprising find at once. Many expeditions therefore use both.

E. Mapping is the other great challenge. Radio waves do not travel far through water, so satellites can only estimate the shape of the seabed from tiny variations in the height of the sea surface. Detailed maps need sound. Ships send out pulses and time the returning echoes. At the pace of the past century, charting the entire seabed in this way would have taken centuries, and by the early 2020s only about a quarter of it had been mapped in high resolution. An international project now aims to complete the picture by combining data from thousands of ships.

F. The reasons to explore go beyond curiosity. The seabed holds lumps of metal, called nodules, which contain materials used in batteries. Companies are interested in mining them, but biologists warn that the slow-growing communities of animals that live there might take decades or longer to recover, if they recover at all. Deep-sea organisms are also studied by medical researchers, because some of them produce chemicals that may prove useful in treating disease.

G. Scientists therefore face a dilemma. They want to learn what lives in the deep before human activity disturbs it. Many argue that mapping and monitoring should come before any large-scale mining, so that decisions are based on evidence rather than guesswork. As technology improves, new species are being described at a steady rate, and each expedition tends to find animals that are new to science. The deep sea may be far from everyday life, but its health could matter to everyone.

items.q: There is no sunlight at all below about 1,000 metres.
items.vi: Đoạn A: dưới khoảng 1.000 mét hoàn toàn không có ánh sáng.

items.q: In the nineteenth century, most scientists expected to find living things in the deepest water.
items.vi: Đoạn B: nhiều người tin rằng không sinh vật nào sống được ở vùng nước tối và lạnh sâu bên dưới.

items.q: Few crewed dives to the deepest point took place in the decades after 1960.
items.vi: Đoạn B: sau chuyến lặn năm 1960, trong nhiều thập kỷ chỉ có rất ít chuyến lặn có người lái.

items.q: Hydrothermal vents were first found in the Atlantic Ocean.
items.vi: Đoạn C: các miệng phun thủy nhiệt được tìm thấy ở đáy Thái Bình Dương.

items.q: Chemosynthetic bacteria are found only near hydrothermal vents.
items.vi: Bài không nói vi khuẩn hóa tổng hợp chỉ có ở gần các miệng phun hay cả nơi khác.

items.q: Which paragraph compares two types of underwater vehicle?
items.vi: Đoạn D so sánh ROV (có cáp, điều khiển từ tàu) với AUV (không cáp, đi theo lộ trình lập trình sẵn).

items.q: Which paragraph explains why satellites cannot map the seabed in detail?
items.vi: Đoạn E: sóng vô tuyến không truyền xa trong nước nên bản đồ chi tiết cần dùng âm thanh.

items.q: Which paragraph describes a discovery that changed ideas about where life can exist?
items.vi: Đoạn C: phát hiện về sinh vật sống nhờ hóa chất cho thấy sự sống không phụ thuộc vào Mặt Trời.

items.q: Which paragraph describes concern about the environmental effects of a possible industry?
items.vi: Đoạn F: các nhà sinh vật học lo rằng khai thác quặng sẽ khiến quần thể sinh vật khó phục hồi.

items.q: Why is deep-sea exploration so difficult?
options: Extreme conditions make the work technically difficult and costly.
Ships cannot stay in one place for long.
Deep water is full of dangerous animals.
items.vi: Đoạn A: bóng tối, lạnh và áp suất cực lớn khiến việc thám hiểm khó và tốn kém.

items.q: What is one advantage of AUVs over ROVs?
options: They react quickly to unexpected finds.
They can collect samples with mechanical arms.
They send live video to the ship.
They can survey large areas cheaply.
items.vi: Đoạn D: AUV có thể khảo sát vùng rộng với chi phí thấp, nhưng khó phản ứng với điều bất ngờ.

items.q: What does the writer say about the international mapping project?
options: It uses satellites instead of sound.
It has mapped most of the seabed already.
It combines data from many ships.
It will be finished within a few years.
items.vi: Đoạn E: dự án quốc tế gộp dữ liệu từ hàng nghìn tàu; mới khoảng một phần tư đáy biển được lập bản đồ chi tiết.

items.q: What is the concern of biologists about mining nodules?
options: Animal communities could take a very long time to recover.
The metals will become too expensive.
Mining ships may be damaged by pressure.
items.vi: Đoạn F: quần thể động vật phát triển chậm có thể mất hàng chục năm hoặc hơn để phục hồi.

items.q: What is the main idea of paragraph G?
options: Scientists have already found all deep-sea species.
New technology no longer improves exploration.
Mining should be banned for ever.
Decisions about the deep sea should be based on knowledge gained first.
items.vi: Đoạn G: nên lập bản đồ và theo dõi trước khi khai thác để quyết định dựa trên bằng chứng.

parts.instr: Write at least 150 words.
parts.instrVi: Viết ít nhất 150 từ (Task 1).

items.text:
The table shows the percentage of commuters in the city of Karsfeld who used five different ways of travelling to work in 1995, 2005 and 2015.

Mode of transport: 1995 / 2005 / 2015
Car: 62% / 58% / 44%
Bus: 21% / 22% / 25%
Train: 9% / 12% / 16%
Bicycle: 4% / 6% / 10%
Walking: 4% / 2% / 5%
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares the proportion of commuters in Karsfeld who used five modes of transport in 1995, 2005 and 2015. Overall, the car remained the most popular choice throughout the period, although its share fell considerably, while the train and the bicycle became more common.

In 1995, 62 percent of commuters travelled by car, and this figure dropped slightly to 58 percent in 2005 before falling sharply to 44 percent in 2015. Bus use, by contrast, rose steadily from 21 percent to 25 percent. The train showed a clearer upward trend, climbing from 9 percent to 12 percent and then to 16 percent, which meant that it nearly doubled over the twenty years.

Cycling was the fastest growing mode in relative terms. Only 4 percent of commuters cycled in 1995, whereas 10 percent did so in 2015. Walking was the least popular option in every year. It accounted for 4 percent at first, fell to 2 percent in 2005, and then recovered to 5 percent by 2015.
items.vi: Bài mẫu Task 1: mở đầu bằng tổng quan (overall), sau đó mô tả xu hướng từng phương tiện, dùng số liệu và từ so sánh như whereas, by contrast.

parts.instr: Write at least 250 words.
parts.instrVi: Viết ít nhất 250 từ (Task 2).

items.q: In many countries, young people now spend a large part of their free time looking at screens, such as phones, tablets and computers. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to solve them? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
items.sample:
It is often said that young people spend too much of their free time looking at screens. In my opinion, this habit does cause real problems, but there are practical solutions that families and schools can adopt.

The most obvious problem is the effect on health. Teenagers who use phones and tablets late at night often go to bed later and sleep badly, which makes it harder to concentrate the next day. Long hours of sitting also reduce the time available for sport and outdoor activities, so fitness can suffer. In addition, spending hours on social media can harm confidence, because young people constantly compare themselves with the carefully chosen images they see online. A further difficulty is that face-to-face communication may weaken. If friends meet but spend the evening looking at their phones, they miss the chance to develop real conversation skills.

There are, however, several ways to deal with these issues. Parents can agree simple rules with their children, such as keeping phones out of the bedroom at night and switching off devices during meals. Schools can also play a part by teaching students how to manage their time online and by organising clubs that offer interesting alternatives, such as music, sport or drama. Technology companies should share responsibility too, for example by offering tools that show users how long they have spent on an app and by limiting notifications after a certain hour.

In conclusion, excessive screen time is a genuine concern for sleep, health and relationships, yet it can be reduced if parents, schools and companies work together. A balanced approach is more realistic than a complete ban, because screens are also useful for study and for staying in touch with family.
items.vi: Bài mẫu Task 2 dạng vấn đề và giải pháp: nêu các vấn đề (sức khỏe, giấc ngủ, giao tiếp), sau đó đề xuất giải pháp từ gia đình, trường học và công ty công nghệ.

parts.instr: Answer the questions about familiar topics.
parts.instrVi: Phần 1: trả lời các câu hỏi về chủ đề quen thuộc.

items.q: Do you enjoy cooking? Why or why not?
items.sample: Yes, I really enjoy cooking because it helps me relax after a long day. I usually make simple dishes like pasta or soup, and sometimes I try new recipes that I find on the internet.
items.vi: Câu trả lời mẫu: thích nấu ăn vì giúp thư giãn, thường nấu món đơn giản và thỉnh thoảng thử công thức mới.

items.q: What do you usually do in the evening?
items.sample: In the evening I usually have dinner with my family and then I watch a series or read for a while. If I have homework, I do it first, and I try to go to bed before eleven o'clock.
items.vi: Câu trả lời mẫu: kể các hoạt động buổi tối như ăn tối cùng gia đình, xem phim, đọc sách, làm bài tập.

items.q: Do you prefer to spend time with friends or on your own?
items.sample: I like both, but it depends on my mood. I enjoy meeting friends at weekends because we can talk and laugh together, although I also need some time on my own to relax and think.
items.vi: Câu trả lời mẫu: thích cả hai tùy tâm trạng, nêu lý do với từ because.

items.q: What kind of music do you like to listen to?
items.sample: I listen to all kinds of music, but mostly pop and a little jazz. Pop songs give me energy when I study, while I like jazz because it is calm, so I often play it before I go to sleep.
items.vi: Câu trả lời mẫu: nói về thể loại nhạc yêu thích và giải thích lý do bằng because.

parts.instr: Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2: nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong 1-2 phút.

items.q: Describe a skill that you learned and that you find useful. You should say: what the skill is, how and where you learned it, who helped you to learn it, and explain why this skill is useful for you.
items.sample: I would like to talk about cooking, which is a skill I learned a few years ago and use almost every day. I learned it at home, in our kitchen, when I was about fifteen. My parents both worked late, so I had to prepare dinner for myself and my younger brother. At first I made many mistakes. I burned the rice, I used too much salt and once I nearly set a pan on fire. My grandmother taught me most of what I know. She lived nearby and visited us at weekends, and she showed me how to cut vegetables safely, how to control the heat and how to taste the food while cooking. She was patient and never laughed at my mistakes. This skill is useful for me for several reasons. First, it saves money, because home food is cheaper than eating out. Second, I can choose healthy ingredients. Finally, cooking has become a way to relax and to share time with my family, so I am very grateful that I learned it.
items.vi: Bài nói mẫu Part 2: nêu kỹ năng (nấu ăn), học ở đâu và như thế nào, ai dạy (bà), và vì sao hữu ích. Chú ý dùng thì quá khứ khi kể và thì hiện tại khi nói về lợi ích.

parts.instr: Discuss the questions about learning skills.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3: thảo luận các câu hỏi trừu tượng về việc học kỹ năng.

items.q: Do you think children learn practical skills better at school or at home?
items.sample: I think both are important, but home is probably better for the basics. Parents can show children how to cook or clean every day, so the learning feels natural. However, schools can give every child the same chances, including those whose parents are too busy to teach them.
items.vi: Câu trả lời mẫu: ở nhà học các kỹ năng cơ bản tự nhiên hơn, nhưng trường học tạo cơ hội bình đẳng cho mọi trẻ.

items.q: Why do some adults find it difficult to learn new skills?
items.sample: Many adults are afraid of failing, so they stop trying too soon. They also have less free time because of work and family, and they do not always have a teacher telling them what to do. Children usually learn faster because they are more curious and less worried about mistakes.
items.vi: Câu trả lời mẫu: người lớn sợ thất bại, ít thời gian và thiếu người hướng dẫn; trẻ em tò mò hơn nên học nhanh hơn.

items.q: How might technology change the way people learn skills in the future?
items.sample: I believe technology will make learning more personal. Apps and videos already let people practise at any time, and in the future artificial intelligence could give feedback to each learner. However, it will still be important to have real teachers who can motivate people and answer difficult questions.
items.vi: Câu trả lời mẫu: công nghệ giúp việc học cá nhân hóa, nhưng giáo viên thật vẫn quan trọng (dùng however để nêu sự đối lập).

parts.instrVi: Hoàn thành biểu mẫu. Viết MỘT TỪ VÀ/HOẶC MỘT SỐ cho mỗi đáp án.

audio.t: Good morning, Eastgate Arts Centre. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like to book a place on one of your weekend pottery courses, please.
Certainly. We have a beginners' course that runs for six weeks, on Saturday mornings.
Does it begin on the fifth of March?
No, the first class is on the twelfth of March. The sessions start at ten o'clock and finish at one.
That sounds good. How much is the course?
It's 168 dollars, and that includes all the clay and the use of the kiln.
Great. Could I have a place, then?
Of course. Can I take your surname?
Yes, it's Lindqvist. That's L, I, N, D, Q, V, I, S, T.
Thank you. And a contact number?
My mobile is 07700 48291.
07700 48291. And your address?
I live at 14 Willow Lane, near the station.
Lovely. You don't need to bring any tools, because we provide those, but please wear an apron or old clothes. Clay can be messy.
I have an apron already. Where can I park?
There's a small car park behind the building, and the entrance is on Mill Street.
Thank you. Oh, and you might like to know that I found out about the course from a poster at the library.
That's useful for us to know. Thank you, Ms Lindqvist. We'll see you on the twelfth.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to this information session about the Halbury Bike Share scheme, which opens to the public next month.

Let me start with where the bikes will be. There will be forty stations across the city, and the first ones will open near the railway station, the university and the riverside market. We had planned to put one outside the hospital as well, but the council has decided to wait until the road there has been repaired, so that station will open in the spring.

Now, the costs. You can pay in two ways. A day pass costs four dollars, while a yearly membership is sixty dollars. The first thirty minutes of every journey are free with both options. After that, you pay one dollar for each extra half hour.

All the bikes have three gears, a basket and lights that switch on automatically. We chose a heavy frame because it is stronger and lasts longer, although some people in our trials told us they would prefer a lighter bike for the hilly streets in the north of the city.
To unlock a bike you use a mobile phone app. If you don't have a smartphone, you can collect a plastic card from the town hall.

A few rules. Riders must be at least sixteen years old. Helmets are not provided, but we are working with a local cycle shop to offer a discount on them. Bikes must always be returned to a station. If you leave one somewhere else, you will be charged a fee of fifteen dollars.

Finally, we still need volunteers to help check the bikes on Saturday mornings. If you are interested, please speak to Mr Tomas at the back of the room. And after the first six months, we will ask all users to complete a survey, and we will use the answers to decide where to add more stations. Thank you.

audio.t: Come in. So, you two have decided on a topic for your history presentation?
Yes, Dr Ellis. We'd like to look at the development of the postal service in the nineteenth century.
That's a rich topic, but it's very broad. What aspect interests you most?
I read that the first stamps appeared in 1840, and that before that the person receiving a letter paid for it, not the sender. I find that fascinating.
I'm more interested in how railways made the service faster. Letters used to go by horse and coach, and then suddenly they crossed the country overnight.
Both are good, but you only have fifteen minutes. I suggest you focus on one country, otherwise you will only skim the surface.
We were thinking of Britain, mainly because most of the sources we found are in English.
Sensible. What sources have you found so far?
Books from the university library, and some online archives of letters. The trouble is that the archives contain very few letters from ordinary people.
That's a common problem, because ordinary people wrote fewer letters and fewer survived. You might find local newspapers useful. They often reported on changes to the postal service in their town.
Good idea. How should we organize the presentation?
Telling the story in date order is the safest plan, but I would start with a single letter, perhaps one from an emigrant to his family, to catch the audience's attention.
We could do that. What about the slides?
Keep the text to a minimum. A picture or a map says more than a paragraph. And prepare a one-page handout with the key dates, so that people don't have to write them down.
When do you need the slides?
Send them to me by Thursday, not Friday, so that I have time to give you feedback.
Thank you, Dr Ellis. That's very helpful.

audio.t: Good morning. Today I'm going to talk about how volcanic islands form, and I'll use the Hawaiian chain as my main example.

Most volcanoes occur at the edges of tectonic plates, but Hawaii is unusual because it lies near the middle of the Pacific Plate. It sits above a hotspot, a place where an extremely hot plume of rock rises from deep inside the Earth.

The plate slowly moves to the northwest at about seven centimeters a year. As it moves, each volcano is carried away from the hotspot and eventually dies, while a new volcano begins to grow over the hotspot.
This is why the islands form a line. The oldest islands are in the northwest of the chain, and the youngest, the Big Island, is at the southeastern end.

Once a volcano stops erupting, erosion begins. Wind, rain and waves wear the island down, and the land also sinks under its own weight. After millions of years, the island may be only a low ring of coral around a lagoon, which we call an atoll.
This explanation was first proposed by Charles Darwin, in 1842, after his long voyage on a research ship.
New islands can still be born. In 1963, an undersea eruption near Iceland created the island of Surtsey, which rose out of the sea within days.

Scientists have used Surtsey as a natural laboratory. The first plant to grow there, in 1965, was a plant called sea rocket, and later the droppings of seabirds added nutrients to the soil, which allowed more species to settle.
To protect this experiment, no tourists are allowed on the island. Only scientists may visit Surtsey. Thank you.

parts.instr: Read the passage about plastic in the oceans and answer questions 1-13.
parts.instrVi: Đọc bài về rác nhựa trong đại dương và trả lời câu hỏi 1-13.

items.text:
A
Every year, millions of tons of plastic enter the world's oceans. Much of it comes from the land: bottles, bags and food packaging are dropped in streets, blown out of waste sites or carried to the sea by rivers. Studies suggest that a small number of large rivers carry a high proportion of the waste, but because the material travels so far on ocean currents, the problem belongs to everyone.

B
Once in the sea, plastic does not rot. Instead, sunlight and waves break it into smaller and smaller pieces. Fragments less than five millimeters long are called microplastics, and they have been found everywhere, from the surface of the water to the mud on the deepest sea floor. Because they are so small, they are almost impossible to remove with nets. Some are made tiny on purpose, such as the little beads once added to face cleaners, while others are fibers shed by synthetic clothes every time they are washed.

C
Marine animals suffer in several ways. Turtles may mistake floating bags for jellyfish, and seabirds sometimes feed pieces of plastic to their chicks. Larger animals become tangled in old fishing nets, known as ghost gear, which can go on trapping fish for years after they were lost. Dr Helena Marsh, who has studied seabirds on the remote Karvik Islands, reports that she found plastic in the stomachs of nearly nine out of ten of the birds she examined. Perhaps more worrying is the possibility that microplastics move up the food chain to people, although researchers are still debating how much harm they do to human health.

D
Cleaning the oceans is difficult. Floating barriers and collection ships have been tested, and they can remove large objects from rivers and calm bays. In the open ocean, however, the waste is spread thinly over enormous areas, and a ship would burn a large amount of fuel to collect only a small amount of plastic. Many experts therefore argue that it is more effective to stop plastic reaching the water in the first place.

E
Several approaches are being tried. Some countries have banned thin plastic bags or introduced a small charge for them, and in the coastal city of Valdoria the number of bags found on beaches fell by more than half within two years of such a charge. Deposit schemes, in which shoppers pay a little extra for a bottle and get the money back when they return it, have produced return rates above ninety percent in places where they operate. Meanwhile, engineers are developing packaging made from seaweed and plant starch that breaks down in weeks rather than centuries. Critics warn, however, that labels such as "biodegradable" can be misleading, since some materials only break down in industrial composting plants and not in the sea.

F
Individuals also have a part to play, but most researchers agree that personal choices alone are not enough. Better waste collection in fast-growing cities, improved recycling systems and rules that make companies responsible for the packaging they produce are all necessary. Without such measures, one widely quoted estimate suggests that by 2050 the weight of plastic in the sea could be greater than the weight of the fish. Whether that happens will depend on the decisions that governments, businesses and ordinary people take now.

parts.instr: Read the passage about the invention of printing and answer questions 14-26.
parts.instrVi: Đọc bài về sự ra đời của nghề in và trả lời câu hỏi 14-26.

items.text:
A
Long before printing arrived in Europe, readers in East Asia were already using it. By about the eighth century, craftsmen in China were carving text and pictures into wooden blocks, covering them with ink and pressing paper against the surface. The oldest printed book with a date, a Buddhist text known as the Diamond Sutra, was produced in China in the year 868. Woodblock printing suited religious texts and calendars well, but every page needed a fresh block, and a single mistake could mean cutting the whole block again.

B
A solution came around 1040, when a man named Bi Sheng is said to have made individual characters from baked clay that could be arranged, inked and used again. Later, printers in Korea improved on the idea by casting characters in metal, and a Korean Buddhist book printed in 1377 is the oldest surviving book made in this way. Yet movable type did not spread quickly in East Asia. One important reason is that the Chinese script uses thousands of different characters, so a printer needed an enormous store of type and a great deal of time to find each piece.

C
In Europe the situation was different. The alphabet has only a few dozen letters, so a small set of metal type could be rearranged to print any text. Around 1450, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg in the German city of Mainz combined several existing technologies into a single system. He designed a hand mold that could cast large numbers of identical letters from a metal mixture, developed an oil-based ink that stuck well to metal, and adapted the screw press used by farmers to squeeze grapes and olives. His most famous product, a large Bible, appeared in about 1455.

D
The effect was dramatic. Before printing, every book was copied by hand, usually by monks, and a single volume might take months to finish. A printing workshop could produce hundreds of copies of the same book in the same time. Prices fell, and books that had once been owned only by churches, universities and the very rich came within reach of merchants and craftsmen. By 1500, printing presses were operating in more than two hundred European towns, and historians estimate that millions of books had been produced.

E
Printing changed more than the book trade. Scholars could now compare identical copies of a text, which helped them find errors and share discoveries quickly. Scientists published diagrams and tables that stayed the same from one copy to the next. Reformers and writers reached large audiences with cheap pamphlets, and rulers soon realized that printed ideas could be hard to control. Some authorities introduced licenses and lists of forbidden books. Literacy also rose gradually, as more people had a reason to learn to read, although it took centuries for reading to become common.

F
Some historians warn against telling the story as a simple tale of one great inventor. Gutenberg's workshop was a business that depended on investors, and he lost control of it after a legal dispute with a creditor. Others point out that printing did not replace handwriting overnight; for decades, wealthy buyers still ordered hand-copied books. Nevertheless, there is little doubt that by making texts cheap and identical, printing helped to lay the foundations of modern education, science and public debate.

parts.instr: Read the passage about motivation at work and answer questions 27-40.
parts.instrVi: Đọc bài về động lực trong công việc và trả lời câu hỏi 27-40.

items.text:
A
Why do some employees arrive at work eager to begin, while others count the minutes until they can leave? Managers have asked this question for over a century, and the answers have changed considerably as societies and workplaces have changed. In the early twentieth century, factory owners assumed that workers were motivated mainly by money, and many paid by the piece. Workers who produced more earned more, and this system did raise output in simple, repetitive jobs.

B
By the 1950s, however, researchers had begun to question the idea. The psychologist Frederick Herzberg interviewed accountants and engineers and concluded that factors such as salary and working conditions could prevent unhappiness but did not by themselves create enthusiasm. Real satisfaction, he argued, came from the work itself: achievement, recognition and responsibility. Although his methods have been criticized, his claim that pay and motivation are not the same thing remains influential.

C
Modern research often distinguishes between extrinsic motivation, which comes from outside rewards such as bonuses, and intrinsic motivation, which comes from interest in the task itself. Professor Lena Okafor of Brenmoor University and her colleagues ran an experiment in which volunteers solved a series of tasks. Those offered a large cash prize for speed did better on a simple mechanical task, but worse on tasks that needed creative thinking. Her explanation is that a strong focus on a reward narrows attention, leaving less room for imaginative ideas.

D
Many psychologists now emphasize three basic needs: autonomy, mastery and purpose. Autonomy is the sense of having some control over how and when work is done; mastery is the satisfaction of getting better at something; and purpose is the belief that the work contributes to something larger than oneself. A software firm in the town of Aldermere that allowed its developers to spend one afternoon a week on projects of their own choice reported that several of its most successful products began as these side projects.

E
Not everyone is convinced. Critics point out that most people need to earn a living, and that praising passion can be used to justify low pay or long hours. A worker who is anxious about paying the rent is unlikely to be inspired by a mission statement. Furthermore, what motivates one person may leave another cold: some employees value flexibility above all, while others want a clear career ladder. For this reason, many managers have moved away from one-size-fits-all schemes.

F
Practical advice therefore tends to be modest. Fair pay should be treated as a starting point rather than a prize. Managers can offer feedback that is specific and timely, give people some choice over how they complete their tasks, and explain how each job fits into the goals of the organization. Small gestures, such as thanking staff by name for a job well done, appear to matter more than many leaders expect. Ultimately, motivation is not something that can be installed in employees; it is more often the result of the conditions in which they work.

parts.instr: You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. The table shows information about visitors to museums.
parts.instrVi: Bạn nên dành khoảng 20 phút cho bài này. Bảng cho biết số lượt khách tham quan các bảo tàng.

items.text:
The table shows the number of visitors, in thousands, to five museums in the city of Carrow in 2010 and in 2023.
City History Museum: 420 in 2010, 510 in 2023.
Science Center: 380 in 2010, 610 in 2023.
Maritime Museum: 250 in 2010, 190 in 2023.
Art Gallery: 300 in 2010, 330 in 2023.
Toy Museum: 90 in 2010, 175 in 2023.
Total for the five museums: 1440 in 2010, 1815 in 2023.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample: The table compares the number of visitors to five museums in Carrow in 2010 and 2023. Overall, the total rose from 1440 thousand to 1815 thousand, and four of the five museums attracted more people at the end of the period. The most striking change was at the Science Center. Its visitors increased from 380 thousand to 610 thousand, which made it the most popular museum in 2023 instead of the City History Museum. The City History Museum also grew, but more slowly, from 420 thousand to 510 thousand. The Toy Museum was the smallest museum in both years, yet its numbers almost doubled, from 90 thousand to 175 thousand. The Art Gallery saw only a modest rise, from 300 thousand to 330 thousand. In contrast, the Maritime Museum was the only one to lose visitors. Its figure fell from 250 thousand to 190 thousand. In summary, science and history attracted the largest audiences, while the Maritime Museum became less popular over the period.
items.vi: Nêu tổng quan (tổng lượt tăng từ 1440 lên 1815), điểm nổi bật (Science Center tăng mạnh nhất, Maritime Museum là bảo tàng duy nhất giảm) và so sánh số liệu.

parts.instr: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.
parts.instrVi: Bạn nên dành khoảng 40 phút cho bài này.

items.q: In many countries the proportion of older people in the population is increasing. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
items.sample:
In many countries people are living longer and having fewer children, so the number of older citizens is growing. In my opinion, this trend brings both benefits and difficulties, but with good planning the advantages can be greater than the disadvantages.

The most obvious problem is the cost to society. Older people usually need more medical care, and pensions have to be paid by a smaller number of working adults. As a result, governments may have to raise taxes or increase the retirement age, which can make younger workers unhappy. In addition, some towns may find it hard to provide enough nurses and suitable housing.

However, there are several important advantages. First, older people have a great deal of knowledge and experience. Many of them continue to work part time, start small businesses or train younger colleagues, and in this way they help the economy rather than only costing money. Second, they give time to their communities. Grandparents often look after children, which allows parents to go out to work, and retired people are among the most active volunteers in schools, hospitals and local clubs. Third, a longer life is in itself a sign of progress, because it shows that health care, food and living conditions have improved.

In my own family, my grandfather will retire at sixty-five but already teaches music twice a week. His students love him, and he says that the work keeps him healthy and happy.

To make the most of this change, governments should encourage flexible working for older people, invest in preventive health care and build housing that is suitable for all ages. If they do so, an older population can be a valuable resource rather than a burden.

In conclusion, although ageing societies face real financial challenges, I believe that the experience, time and energy of older people mean that the advantages are greater.
items.vi: Bài luận thảo luận hai mặt: nêu bất lợi (chi phí y tế, lương hưu) và lợi ích (kinh nghiệm, đóng góp cộng đồng), rồi đưa ra quan điểm rõ ràng ở phần kết.

parts.instr: Part 2: Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2: Nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong một đến hai phút.

items.q: Describe a skill that you learned from another person. You should say: what the skill was, who taught it to you, how you learned it, and explain why this skill is useful to you.
items.sample: I would like to talk about swimming, which is a skill I learned from my uncle when I was nine years old. My uncle lives near a small lake, and every summer he took me there at the weekend. At first I was afraid of deep water, so he started in the shallow part and showed me how to float on my back. He was very patient. He never laughed when I made mistakes, and he always praised me when I improved. After about two months, I could swim across the lake with him next to me in a small boat. I learned mostly by practicing again and again, and by watching how he moved his arms and legs. This skill is useful to me for several reasons. Firstly, it keeps me fit, because I swim twice a week at the city pool. Secondly, it makes me feel safe near water when I go on holiday. Finally, it reminds me of my uncle and the happy summers we spent together, which is why I value it so much. He taught me that patience and regular practice are the secret of learning anything new.
items.vi: Nói theo 4 ý của thẻ gợi ý: kỹ năng, người dạy, cách học và lý do hữu ích; dùng thì quá khứ và từ nối.

parts.instr: Part 3: Discuss some more general questions on the same theme.

items.q: Why do some people find it easier to learn new skills than others?
items.sample: I think there are several reasons. Some people have stronger motivation, so they practice more often and do not give up easily. Others learned good study habits when they were young. Of course, a good teacher also makes a big difference, because clear explanations save a lot of time.
items.vi: Nêu nhiều nguyên nhân (động lực, thói quen, giáo viên) và giải thích bằng 'because'.

items.q: Do you think it is better to learn a skill from a teacher or from the internet?
items.sample: Both have advantages. A teacher can correct your mistakes immediately and explain things in different ways. The internet, however, is cheaper and you can learn at your own speed. In my opinion, beginners should start with a teacher, and later they can use the internet to practice more.
items.vi: So sánh hai cách học và đưa ra quan điểm cá nhân, dùng 'however'.

items.q: How will the way people learn change in the future?
items.sample: In the future, I think technology will play a bigger role in education. Students will probably use virtual classrooms and personal programs that adapt to their level. However, I believe that teachers will still be important, because learners need encouragement and human contact.
items.vi: Dự đoán tương lai với 'will/probably' và nêu vai trò của công nghệ.

Certainly. We have a beginners' course for adults starting on March the 14th. It was going to start on the 7th, but we've had to move it by a week.
That's fine. How long does it run?
Six weeks. Could I have your surname?
It's Okafor. That's O-K-A-F-O-R.
Thank you. And a contact number?
My mobile is 07700 913 468.
Thank you, 468 at the end. Now, the class is on Saturday mornings. There's also a Sunday class, but it's full.
Saturday is perfect. What time does it start?
At ten o'clock, and it finishes at half past twelve. Please arrive about ten minutes early.

One hundred and twenty dollars for the six weeks. That includes the clay, but not the glazes, which are extra. Last year it was a hundred, but prices have gone up.
OK. Is there anything I need to bring?

And where do I go?
Studio 3, on the second floor. Studio 2 is for the advanced class, so please don't go there by mistake.

Great, thanks very much.

audio.t: Good evening everyone, and welcome to the reopening of Fernhill Leisure Centre. My name is Carol Whitby and I am the manager. Before you explore the building, I'd like to explain what has changed during the last eighteen months.

The centre first opened in 1975 and, by last year, the roof was leaking and the heating failed regularly. The council therefore decided to close it for repairs rather than build a new one, mainly because the old building has a distinctive design that local people love.

The biggest change is the swimming pool. It is now twenty-five metres long instead of twenty, and we have added a shallow pool for toddlers, which was the most popular request in our local survey. There is also a moving floor, so we can make part of the main pool shallower for lessons.

Next, the gym. We have doubled the number of machines, but we have not raised prices. Current members keep their old rates, and new members pay twenty-eight dollars a month. Students and people over sixty-five pay half.
Now the cafe. It is on the first floor and has a terrace with a view of the park. We have chosen a local family firm to run it, so most of the ingredients come from farms within thirty miles.
On opening hours: the centre will open at six in the morning on weekdays, so that people can swim before work, and it closes at ten at night. On Sundays it opens later, at eight, and closes at six.
Parking is limited. We have only sixty spaces, so we ask you to cycle or take the number 14 bus, which now stops right outside. We have installed a covered rack for a hundred bicycles.

Finally, volunteers. We need people to help with children's swimming lessons on Saturday mornings. You don't need any special qualifications, because we will provide training, but you must be over eighteen. If you are interested, please leave your name at the front desk before you leave tonight. Now, please enjoy the tour.

items.q: Why did the council repair the centre instead of building a new one?
options: The old roof was still in good condition.
Local people like the design of the building.
There was no land available for a new centre.
It would have been cheaper to rebuild it.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, you're here to talk about your fieldwork report on coastal erosion?
Yes, Dr Hale. We spent three days at Marram Point in October, measuring the cliff edge.
We chose Marram Point because our first idea, Gull Beach, was closed for safety reasons after a landslide.
A sensible change. What method did you use for measuring?
We planned to use a drone, but the wind was too strong on the first day, so we used measuring tapes and stakes at fifteen fixed points.
Good. And what did you find?
The cliff has retreated by an average of one point two metres since the last survey in 2019, which is more than we expected.
The worst section was near the stream, where water runs down the face of the cliff. I think that's more important than the waves.
Interesting, but be careful. Did you check the rainfall records?
Not yet. We only looked at the storm records.
Then I'd suggest you add the rainfall data. A report that considers only one cause may look weak.
Right. We also interviewed some residents. One farmer told us he has lost three metres of field in ten years.
That's useful local evidence, but remember it's one person's memory, so you must make clear it isn't measured data.
Should we put it in the main results or in an appendix?
I'd put it in the discussion section, as support for your own measurements.
What about the graphs? Mia wants one graph for each measuring point, but I think that's too many.
Fifteen graphs would be confusing, I agree. Perhaps a single map with coloured arrows?
Yes, a map with arrows showing the amount of retreat would be much clearer. Then put the table of figures in the appendix.
And the word limit is three thousand words?
Yes, and I'd rather you spent them on analysis than on describing the site. Keep the introduction to two hundred words.
When is the deadline?
The twelfth of December, but I'd like to see a draft by the end of November.
Should we bring it in, or send it by email?
Email is fine, but please book a short meeting afterwards so that I can talk you through my comments.
Thank you, Dr Hale. We will.

items.q: Why did the students change their location from Gull Beach?
options: It was closed after a landslide.
It was too far to travel.
It had no cliffs to measure.
items.vi: Bãi Gull bị đóng cửa vì lý do an toàn sau một vụ lở đất.

items.q: Why did they not use a drone?
options: The university did not allow it.
items.vi: Ngày đầu tiên gió quá mạnh nên họ dùng thước dây và cọc.

items.q: How many measuring points did they use?
items.vi: Họ đo tại 15 điểm cố định.

items.q: How far has the cliff retreated on average since 2019?
items.vi: Vách đá lùi trung bình 1,2 mét kể từ năm 2019 (3 mét là lời của người nông dân).

items.q: What does Mia think is the main cause near the stream?
items.vi: Mia cho rằng nước chảy xuống mặt vách đá quan trọng hơn sóng.

items.q: What does Dr Hale advise them to add?
items.vi: Thầy khuyên thêm số liệu lượng mưa vì chỉ xét một nguyên nhân thì báo cáo yếu.

items.q: What does Dr Hale say about the farmer's comments?
options: They should be left out completely.
They should be used as support in the discussion.
They are the most reliable evidence.
items.vi: Lời nông dân là bằng chứng hữu ích nhưng không phải số liệu đo, nên đặt ở phần thảo luận.

items.q: What does Dr Hale recommend instead of fifteen graphs?
items.vi: Một bản đồ có mũi tên chỉ mức lùi sẽ rõ ràng hơn mười lăm biểu đồ.

items.q: Where should the table of figures go?
items.vi: Bảng số liệu nên đặt trong phần phụ lục.

audio.t: Good morning everyone. Today I'm going to talk about the history of glass, a material so common that we rarely stop to think about where it came from.

Let's start with the basics. Glass is made mainly from sand, which is heated to a very high temperature until it melts. Other substances, such as soda and lime, are added so that the melting happens at a lower temperature.

Glass also exists in nature. When lightning strikes sand, or when a volcano erupts, the heat can create natural glass. The best known is obsidian, a dark, shiny stone that early people used to make knives and arrowheads, because it breaks into very sharp edges.

The first glass objects made by people were small beads and later containers, produced in Mesopotamia about 3,500 years ago. They were made by wrapping soft glass around a core of clay, which was removed afterwards. It was such a slow process that glass was as valuable as precious stones.

A great change came in the first century BC, when craftsmen in the Roman world discovered glassblowing. By blowing air through a tube into a lump of hot glass, they could make thin, light bottles and cups in minutes, and glass became cheap enough for ordinary households.

Now move forward to the Middle Ages. Venice became the centre of glassmaking, but there was a problem, because the furnaces caused many fires. In 1291 the authorities ordered all glassmakers to move to the nearby island of Murano, which also helped them keep their techniques secret. In the fifteenth century one Venetian glassmaker produced a very clear glass that he called cristallo, and it was exported across Europe.
In the seventeenth century, English makers added lead to the mixture. Lead glass is heavier than ordinary glass and has more sparkle, so it became popular for drinking glasses and chandeliers.

For windows, large flat sheets were difficult to make for centuries. This changed in 1959, when a British engineer invented the float process, in which melted glass is poured onto a bath of liquid tin. The glass spreads out and becomes perfectly flat. Nearly all window glass today is made this way.
Today, glass is used in surprising ways. Fibres of glass, thinner than a human hair, carry light signals along optical cables, and so they carry most of the world's internet traffic.
Finally, a word about the environment. One great advantage of glass is that it can be recycled again and again without losing its quality. Thank you for listening.

items.text:
A. Agriculture is among the human activities most sensitive to weather. Unlike a factory, a farm has no roof, and every crop depends on a narrow range of temperature, rainfall and sunshine. Over the past century, average global temperatures have risen by about one degree Celsius, and although that may sound small, it has been enough to shift the growing seasons in many regions. In northern Europe, for example, spring planting now begins up to two weeks earlier than it did in the 1960s, and some farmers have started to harvest a second crop of fast-growing vegetables before winter arrives.

B. Warmer conditions do not benefit every farmer equally. Wheat, one of the world's most important staple crops, grows best in cool climates, and research suggests that each additional degree of warming during the grain-filling period can reduce yields by around six per cent. Rice faces a different problem: it is sensitive to high night-time temperatures, which cause the plant to use up energy that it would otherwise store in its grain. In contrast, crops such as maize and sorghum are more tolerant of heat, but they need reliable rainfall, which is exactly what is becoming less predictable in many tropical countries.

C. Water is the second great uncertainty. A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so when rain does fall it is often heavier, washing away topsoil and flooding fields. Yet long dry periods have also become more common in some areas, forcing farmers to rely on irrigation. About seventy per cent of the fresh water that people take from rivers and underground reserves is already used to grow food, and in regions where those reserves are falling, irrigation cannot be increased indefinitely. The mountain glaciers that feed rivers in South Asia and South America are shrinking, which means that water supplies that seemed permanent may become seasonal within a few decades.

D. Pests and diseases add a further complication. Many insects reproduce faster in warm weather, and species that were once limited to the tropics are moving towards the poles. A fungus that damages bananas, for instance, has been recorded in countries where it was unknown twenty years ago. Farmers must therefore spend more on pesticides, or find new ways of protecting their plants. Some researchers believe that the answer lies in encouraging natural predators, such as ladybirds, to live around the fields, rather than in using more chemicals.

E. Fortunately, farmers and scientists are not standing still. Plant breeders are developing varieties of wheat and rice that tolerate heat and drought, using both traditional crossing methods and modern genetic tools. In one project in East Africa, small farmers received seeds of a bean that matures in sixty days instead of ninety, allowing the crop to finish before the dry season begins. Simple changes can also make a difference: planting trees beside fields to provide shade, covering soil with straw to keep it moist, and collecting rainwater in underground tanks have all raised harvests in dry districts without expensive equipment.

F. Technology is playing a growing part as well. Satellites now measure soil moisture across entire regions, and mobile phone applications send farmers short weather forecasts and advice on when to plant. In a trial in southern India, farmers who received such messages increased their income by an average of eleven per cent compared with neighbors who did not. Critics, however, point out that these services are of little use to people without phones or electricity, and that the poorest farmers, who have contributed least to climate change, are often the least able to adapt to it.

G. Looking ahead, most experts agree that no single solution will be enough. Food systems will have to combine new crops, better water management, and fairer access to information and credit. Changing diets may help too: producing a kilogram of beef requires many times more land and water than producing a kilogram of beans. The challenge is considerable, but the experience of recent decades shows that agriculture has always adapted to new conditions, and that, with support, it can do so again.

items.text:
A. Every day, a person makes thousands of decisions, most of them so small that they barely seem like choices: which route to take to work, what to eat for lunch, whether to answer a message now or later. Psychologists who study decision-making have found that people are far less rational than they believe. Rather than weighing every option carefully, we rely on mental shortcuts, known as heuristics, which allow us to act quickly but sometimes lead us into predictable mistakes.

B. The best-known research on this subject was carried out by two psychologists in the 1970s. They showed that the way a choice is described can change what people choose, even when the facts are identical. In one famous experiment, volunteers were told about a disease threatening six hundred people and were asked to choose between two treatments. When the options were described in terms of lives saved, most people preferred the safe option. When exactly the same options were described in terms of lives lost, most chose the risky one. This "framing effect" suggests that people feel losses more strongly than equal gains.

C. Another common error is anchoring. When people must estimate a number, they tend to be influenced by any figure they have recently heard, even if it is clearly irrelevant. In one study, participants spun a wheel marked with numbers and were then asked how many African countries belonged to an international organization. Those whose wheel had stopped at a high number gave much higher estimates than those whose wheel had stopped at a low number. Shops make use of this tendency when they display a high "original" price next to a sale price, which makes the sale price look like a bargain.

D. Emotion also plays a larger part than most people admit. A neurologist who studied patients with damage to the part of the brain that links emotion and reasoning reported a surprising result: these patients could analyze problems perfectly well, but they struggled to make even simple decisions, such as choosing a date for an appointment. Without feelings to guide them, they went on listing advantages and disadvantages for hours. It seems, therefore, that emotion is not the enemy of good judgment but a necessary part of it.

E. A further problem is the number of options available. Many shoppers believe that more choice is always better, yet experiments suggest otherwise. In a well-known study in a food shop, a table offering twenty-four types of jam attracted more visitors than one offering six, but customers were about ten times more likely to buy from the smaller display. Researchers explain that a large selection makes people worry about missing the perfect option, and this anxiety can lead them to postpone the decision altogether, or to feel less satisfied with what they finally choose.

F. Can people learn to decide better? Evidence suggests that they can, though not by trying to become purely logical. One useful technique is to consider a decision from an outsider's point of view, by asking, "What would I advise a friend to do?" Another is to make important choices when one is rested, since tiredness and hunger both reduce the quality of judgment; a widely reported study of judges found that they were more likely to approve requests at the start of the day and just after meals. Some organizations also use a "pre-mortem", in which a team imagines that a project has failed and then lists the reasons why, bringing hidden risks to light before any money is spent.

G. Understanding these patterns has practical value beyond the laboratory. Doctors, teachers and government planners now use findings from psychology to design forms, menus and reminders that help people make choices that are good for them, such as saving for retirement or taking medicine on time. Critics argue that such "nudges" can be a form of manipulation, but supporters reply that every choice must be presented in some way, so it is better to arrange options thoughtfully than by accident. Either way, the study of decisions reminds us that the mind is not a calculating machine but a flexible, and sometimes fallible, tool.

items.q: People usually consider every option carefully before they decide.
items.vi: Đoạn A nói con người ít lý trí hơn họ nghĩ và dựa vào lối tắt tư duy.

items.text:
A. The oldest surviving maps are not drawings of land at all but marks on clay. Tablets made in Mesopotamia more than four thousand years ago show plots of farmland, with measurements written beside them, so that tax collectors and landowners could settle disputes about boundaries. Maps in the ancient world were thus practical tools, produced by officials rather than explorers.

B. The Greeks added theory to practice. Around the sixth century BC, scholars began to argue that the Earth was not flat, and by the third century a librarian in Alexandria had measured its circumference with surprising accuracy, using only the length of shadows at two places and some geometry. Later, a second-century scholar compiled a guide listing the positions of thousands of places, and described a way of drawing curved lines of latitude and longitude on a flat sheet. Although many of his distances were wrong, his idea of a grid influenced mapmakers for more than a thousand years.

C. In medieval Europe, many maps changed purpose. The famous "mappae mundi" were less concerned with routes than with meaning. Jerusalem was placed at the centre, and the edges of the page were filled with strange animals and peoples described in old stories. Such maps were not intended to help travelers; they were teaching tools which showed how a scholar understood the history of the world. Meanwhile, sailors in the Mediterranean used a different type of chart, covered with straight lines radiating from compass points and marked with the names of ports. These "portolan" charts were remarkably accurate for coastlines and were handed down from captain to captain.

D. The age of exploration in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries created a demand for maps that could be used on long ocean voyages. The difficulty was that a sphere cannot be flattened without distortion. In 1569 a Flemish mapmaker solved one problem by designing a projection in which lines of constant compass direction appear straight, so that a navigator could simply draw a line between two ports and follow a single bearing. The price of this convenience was that areas near the poles appeared much larger than they really are, an effect that still shapes how many people imagine the size of countries today.

E. The invention of printing made maps cheaper and more widely available, and by the seventeenth century, collections of maps bound into books, called atlases, had become fashionable among wealthy merchants. But accuracy was limited by the difficulty of measuring longitude. Latitude could be found by observing the sun or stars, but longitude required accurate knowledge of the time at a fixed place, and no clock could keep time at sea. After a series of shipwrecks, a government in Britain offered a large prize in 1714 for a practical solution, and a self-taught clockmaker eventually produced a watch that kept steady time through months of rough voyages.

F. On land, the next advance was systematic surveying. In the eighteenth century, teams in France began measuring a chain of triangles across the whole country, using precise instruments to calculate distances from a single carefully measured baseline. The resulting map took several generations to complete but was far more accurate than any before it, and other nations soon followed. Military leaders were among the most eager customers, since a reliable map could decide the outcome of a campaign.

G. In the twentieth century, aerial photography and then satellites transformed mapmaking again. A photograph taken from an aircraft can record more detail in a few seconds than a surveyor could collect in a year, and signals from satellites now allow anyone with a phone to find their position within a few meters. Digital maps can also be updated continuously: traffic delays, new roads and even the opening hours of shops appear almost as soon as they change.

H. Yet the history of maps also contains a warning. Every map is a selection, and what it shows reveals the interests of its maker. Early tax maps recorded only what could be taxed; medieval charts recorded what people believed; modern navigation applications highlight businesses that pay to be seen. Understanding who made a map, and why, remains as important as reading its symbols.

parts.instr: You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. Write at least 150 words.
parts.instrVi: Bạn nên dành khoảng 20 phút cho bài này. Viết ít nhất 150 từ.

items.text:
The table shows how employees in four towns travelled to work in 2024 (percentage of all journeys).

Ashford: car 62%, bus 18%, train 5%, bicycle 10%, walking 5%.
Brindle: car 41%, bus 25%, train 14%, bicycle 12%, walking 8%.
Corley: car 28%, bus 20%, train 30%, bicycle 15%, walking 7%.
Dunmore: car 55%, bus 12%, train 3%, bicycle 8%, walking 22%.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample: The table compares the ways in which workers in four towns travelled to work in 2024. Overall, the car was the most popular choice in three of the towns, whereas the train was the main method in Corley. Car use was highest in Ashford, at 62%, followed by Dunmore at 55%. In Brindle, 41% of workers drove, while only 28% did so in Corley, which was the lowest figure. Public transport showed a very different pattern. In Corley, 30% of people took the train and a further 20% took the bus, so half of all journeys used public transport. By contrast, only 3% of Dunmore's workers used the train, and just 5% of Ashford's. Buses were most common in Brindle, at 25%, although Ashford was not far behind at 18%. Cycling was most popular in Corley, at 15%, and least popular in Dunmore, at 8%. Walking was relatively unusual in most towns, accounting for between 5% and 8% of journeys, but it stood out in Dunmore, where 22% of employees walked to work. In summary, private cars dominated travel in Ashford and Dunmore, while Corley relied much more on trains and buses, and Brindle had the most balanced mixture of transport methods.
items.vi: Bài Task 1: nêu xu hướng chung, so sánh số liệu giữa các thị trấn (ô tô cao nhất ở Ashford, tàu hỏa nổi bật ở Corley), dùng từ nối như whereas, by contrast.

parts.instr: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.
parts.instrVi: Bạn nên dành khoảng 40 phút cho bài này. Viết ít nhất 250 từ.

items.q: Some people believe that museums and galleries should be free for everyone and paid for by the government. Others think that visitors should pay for their own tickets. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
items.sample:
In many countries, there is a debate about whether museums and galleries should be free to enter. Some people think that the government should pay for them, while others believe that visitors should buy tickets. In this essay I will discuss both views, and I will explain why I partly agree with each of them.

Those who support free entry argue that museums belong to everyone. If tickets are expensive, families on low incomes may never visit, and children may miss the chance to learn about science, history and art. Free admission also encourages people to make short, repeated visits, for example to see only one gallery during a lunch break, instead of feeling that they must spend a whole day inside to get value for money. In several cities where entry charges were removed, the number of visitors rose sharply, and many of the new visitors were young people.

However, there are good reasons for charging a fee. Museums are costly to run, because they must protect valuable objects, employ experts and keep large buildings warm and safe. Governments have many other demands on their budgets, such as hospitals, schools and roads, and some taxpayers may feel that they should not pay for a service that they never use. Money from tickets can also give a museum more independence, so that it can organize new exhibitions without waiting for official approval.

In my opinion, the best solution is a mixture of both systems. Permanent collections could be free, so that everyone can enjoy the most important objects in the national heritage, while special exhibitions could require a ticket. In addition, museums could offer free days for students and low-cost passes for local residents. This approach would protect fair access to culture and, at the same time, provide extra income.

In conclusion, although there are strong arguments on both sides, I believe that public money should keep the basic collections open to all, and that visitors who want a special experience can reasonably be asked to pay for it.
items.vi: Bài Task 2 dạng thảo luận hai quan điểm và nêu ý kiến: có mở bài, hai đoạn thân bài cho hai quan điểm, đoạn nêu ý kiến riêng và kết luận.

parts.instr: Part 1: Answer the questions about familiar topics.
parts.instrVi: Phần 1: Trả lời các câu hỏi về chủ đề quen thuộc.

items.q: Let's talk about your hometown. What do you like most about the place where you live?
items.sample: I come from a small coastal town, and what I like most about my hometown is the friendly people. Everyone knows each other, and it is very easy to make friends there, because the community is so close.
items.vi: Câu hỏi Part 1 về quê hương: nêu điều bạn thích nhất và đưa lý do.

items.q: Do you enjoy cooking? Why or why not?
items.sample: Yes, I really enjoy cooking, mostly because it helps me relax after a long day. At weekends I often make dinner for my family, and we all sit down together, which is something I enjoy a lot.
items.vi: Câu hỏi Part 1 về nấu ăn: trả lời Yes/No và giải thích bằng lý do cụ thể.

items.q: How do you usually spend your evenings?
items.sample: In the evenings I usually do my homework first, and then I read or watch a film. If the weather is nice, I sometimes go for a short walk with my brother before it gets dark.
items.vi: Câu hỏi Part 1 về thói quen buổi tối: dùng trạng từ tần suất như usually, sometimes.

items.q: What kind of music do you like listening to?
items.sample: I like listening to pop music and some classical music as well. I listen to pop when I travel by bus, but I prefer classical music when I study, because it helps me concentrate and stay calm.
items.vi: Câu hỏi Part 1 về âm nhạc: nêu thể loại yêu thích và lý do.

parts.instr: Part 2: Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2: Nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong một đến hai phút.

items.q:
Describe a time when you learned a new skill.
You should say:
- what the skill was
- who or what helped you to learn it
- what difficulties you had
and explain how you felt when you finally learned it.
items.sample: I would like to talk about the time I learned a new skill, swimming, which happened when I was twelve. I had always been a little afraid of deep water, and my friends used to laugh at me at the beach, so one summer I decided to take lessons at the local pool. My teacher was a patient young woman who helped me a great deal. She started by teaching me to float on my back, and then she showed me how to move my arms and legs together. I also watched videos at home, which helped me to understand the technique. The main difficulty was my fear. In the first two weeks I could not put my face in the water, and I often felt like giving up. Another problem was breathing, because I kept swallowing water when I turned my head. However, I practiced twice a week, and slowly I became more confident. When I finally swam one whole length of the pool without stopping, I felt extremely proud and happy. My parents were waiting at the side, and they clapped when I reached the wall. Since then, I have enjoyed swimming at least once a week, and I learned that I can do difficult things if I keep trying.
items.vi: Part 2 (thẻ gợi ý): nói liên tục khoảng 2 phút, đi lần lượt qua các ý trên thẻ: kỹ năng, người giúp đỡ, khó khăn và cảm xúc.

parts.instr: Part 3: Discuss the questions about learning in more depth.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3: Thảo luận sâu hơn các câu hỏi về việc học.

items.q: Why do some people learn new skills more quickly than others?
items.sample: I think there are several reasons. Firstly, some people are more motivated, because they really want to succeed, so they practice more often. Secondly, the way a person was taught makes a big difference. A good teacher can explain things clearly and give useful feedback. Finally, age and experience matter too, since someone who has already learned a similar skill can often learn a new one faster.
items.vi: Part 3: đưa ra nhiều lý do (động lực, cách dạy, kinh nghiệm) và dùng từ nối firstly, secondly, finally.

items.q: Should schools teach more practical skills, such as cooking or managing money?
items.sample: Yes, I believe schools should teach more practical skills. At the moment, many students leave school knowing a lot of theory, but they do not know how to plan a budget or prepare a healthy meal. These skills are useful in everyday life, and young people would feel more independent. Of course, academic subjects are still important, so schools should add practical lessons rather than replace the existing ones.
items.vi: Part 3: nêu quan điểm rõ ràng (should), đưa ví dụ và thừa nhận mặt còn lại của vấn đề.

items.q: How do you think the way people learn will change in the future?
items.sample: I think technology will change learning a great deal in the future. More people will learn online, and they will be able to study at any time and in any place. Computer programs may also adapt lessons to each learner, so that students can go at their own speed. However, I believe teachers will still be necessary, because they can encourage students and help them to solve problems that a program cannot understand.
items.vi: Part 3: dự đoán tương lai với will/may, nêu lợi ích của công nghệ nhưng vẫn khẳng định vai trò của giáo viên.

audio.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Ashdown Valley Heritage Railway. Before we board, let me tell you a little about us.

The line opened in 1871. Many people assume it carried passengers from the start, but it was actually built to carry slate from the quarries in the hills to the port. Passengers were only added about ten years later.

The railway closed in 1968 because most people had started traveling by car. For almost twenty years the tracks were overgrown, until a group of local volunteers decided to bring them back. They reopened the first section in 1987, and today more than two hundred volunteers still work here, from drivers to gardeners.
Our journey today takes fifty-five minutes each way. If you want the best views of the river, sit on the left side of the train, as the right-hand windows mostly look at the forest.
There is no cafe on the train, but you can buy hot drinks and cakes at Millbrook station, where we stop for twenty minutes.
Tickets for adults are twelve dollars, and children between five and sixteen pay six dollars. Children under five travel free.
In December we run special lantern evenings, when the carriages are decorated with lights. Those need to be booked at least two weeks in advance.
If you drove today, you will have seen that the old car park by the entrance is closed for repairs. Please use the new one behind the station.

You are welcome to take photographs anywhere on the train and at the stations. The only place where we ask you not to use a camera is the engine workshop, for safety reasons. Now, please follow me to the platform.
