audio.t: Come in, both of you. Let us talk about your project on how students travel to campus. How far have you got?
We have designed the questionnaire. Our plan was to give it to two hundred students, but we have only collected a hundred and twenty answers so far.
Most of them were collected in the library, which may be a problem, because library users could be unrepresentative of the whole student body.
Good point. You should also collect answers at the cafeteria and the sports center, so that you reach different groups.
We thought of using an online form too.
That is fine for speed, but response rates tend to be low. If you use it, send a reminder after a week.
Our main finding so far is that forty percent of students walk, thirty percent take the bus, and only fifteen percent cycle. We expected more cyclists.
Why do you think that is?
Well, bikes are not that expensive, and the roads are fairly safe. The main reason in the questionnaire is that there is nowhere secure to park a bike on campus.
Interesting. Make sure you include that in your discussion section.
We were wondering about the structure of the report. Should the literature review go after the method?
No, the literature review comes first, right after the introduction. The method follows it.
How many sources should we use?
At least ten, and make sure that half of them are from the last five years.
We found an article about a city that made buses free for students, and ridership doubled.
That would be useful as a comparison, but check how the data was collected. If the sample was small, be careful.
When do you need the draft?

Could we ask the university transport office for figures?

audio.t: Today I want to look at the development of the bicycle, which is one of the most efficient machines ever invented.

The first ancestor of the bicycle appeared in 1817, when a German baron built a wooden machine with two wheels but no pedals. Riders pushed along the ground with their feet, so it was called a running machine. It was popular only for a few years, because roads were rough and it was uncomfortable.

The next important step came in the 1860s, when pedals were fixed to the front wheel. This model was nicknamed the boneshaker, because the frame was made of iron and the wheels were wooden, so riders felt every bump.

Later, to go faster, makers made the front wheel larger, up to a hundred and fifty centimeters across. These high-wheelers were fast but dangerous, because a rider could fall a long way forward over the handlebars.
The real breakthrough was the safety bicycle of the 1880s. It had two wheels of equal size and a chain driving the rear wheel, which allowed a much lower seat.
Then, in 1888, a veterinarian invented air-filled rubber tires, and the ride became far smoother.

By the 1890s the bicycle had become so popular that it changed society. It gave women much greater independence, and some historians argue that it even changed clothing styles, as long skirts were impractical.
In the twentieth century, gears were added, with up to three speeds at first. Today, lightweight frames and electric motors continue to make bicycles more attractive for city travel.

parts.instr: Questions 1-13. Read the passage on artificial intelligence in medicine and answer the questions.
parts.instrVi: Câu 1-13. Đọc bài về trí tuệ nhân tạo trong y học và trả lời câu hỏi.

items.text:
A
For more than a decade, researchers have trained computer programs to recognize patterns in medical images. The first systems were narrow: a program might learn to spot one type of shadow on a chest scan and nothing else. Today's tools are trained on millions of images and can flag several conditions at once. At the Marlowe Regional Hospital, a screening program now reads every chest scan before a doctor does, and marks those that look unusual. Staff say the biggest change is not accuracy but speed, because urgent cases move to the top of the queue within minutes.

B
The reason these programs work so well is the amount of data they can absorb. A human radiologist may study perhaps fifty thousand scans in a long career. A learning program can process that many in a single afternoon, and it never gets tired or distracted. However, it also has a weakness. If most of the training images come from one type of machine or one group of patients, the program may perform poorly on others. A team led by Dr. Ines Calloway found that a skin-cancer tool trained mainly on images of light skin made more mistakes on darker skin, and the problem was only discovered after the tool had been released.

C
Predicting illness before it appears is another growing area. In the town of Westerby, a small clinic uses a program that studies routine records such as blood pressure, age, and past visits to estimate which patients are most likely to develop diabetes within five years. Nurses then invite those patients for advice on diet and exercise. After three years, the clinic reported that fewer people in the high-risk group had developed the disease than expected. The managers are careful to point out, though, that no control group was used, so the contribution of the program cannot be proved.

D
Drug discovery has also changed. Developing a new medicine traditionally takes around ten years and costs a huge sum, partly because most candidate chemicals fail. Computer models can now predict how a molecule will behave in the body before any laboratory work begins, which removes many unpromising candidates early. One pharmaceutical group in the city of Altona says it cut the first stage of its research from four years to eighteen months. Yet the final tests on real patients cannot be skipped, and they still take most of the time.

E
Many doctors welcome these tools but worry about trust. If a program recommends a treatment, the doctor needs to know why. Some systems work like a "black box": they give an answer without any explanation. Dr. Samuel Okonkwo, a heart specialist, argues that a recommendation that cannot be explained is of little use, because he remains legally responsible for every decision he makes. Several companies are therefore building programs that highlight the part of an image that influenced their conclusion, so that a doctor can check it with his or her own eyes.

F
Patients' privacy is the final concern. Training a program requires large numbers of medical records, and even when names are removed, it is sometimes possible to work out who a record belongs to. Hospitals must balance the benefit of better tools against the duty to protect personal information. Most experts expect that the technology will not replace doctors but will change their work, leaving them more time to talk to patients while machines handle repetitive tasks. Whether this promise is kept will depend on how carefully the tools are tested, explained, and regulated.

parts.instr: Questions 14-26. Read the passage on desert ecosystems and answer the questions.
parts.instrVi: Câu 14-26. Đọc bài về hệ sinh thái sa mạc và trả lời câu hỏi.

items.text:
A
To most people, a desert suggests an empty landscape of sand and heat. In fact, a desert is defined by rainfall, not temperature: it is any region that receives less than 250 millimeters of precipitation a year. By this definition, the polar regions also count as deserts. Hot deserts cover about a fifth of the land surface of the planet, and although they look lifeless, many are home to a surprising range of plants and animals that have adapted to survive with very little water. Understanding how they do this has become an important research topic for biologists around the world.

B
Plants have found several different solutions. Cacti store water in thick stems and protect it with sharp spines, which also provide a little shade. Other plants, such as the tarsan bush, grow roots that spread widely just below the surface so that they can capture even a light shower within hours. A third group survives as seeds. These annual plants may lie dormant in the soil for years, then germinate, flower, and set new seed within a few weeks of a heavy rainstorm. Visitors who arrive at the right moment may see a dry plain turn into a carpet of flowers almost overnight.

C
Animals face the same problem and have developed equally varied answers. Many avoid the heat by being active only at night. During the day, small mammals such as the kangaroo rat shelter in cool burrows, where the air is more humid. Remarkably, this animal can live its whole life without drinking, obtaining the water it needs from the seeds it eats. Larger animals cannot hide so easily. Camels tolerate a loss of body water that would be fatal to most mammals, and their body temperature is allowed to rise during the day instead of being controlled by sweating, which saves a great deal of water.

D
The web of life in a desert is delicate because each link depends on a short period of plenty. After rain, insects emerge in large numbers, birds arrive to feed on them, and predators follow the birds. Ecologists studying the Karrow Basin found that a single wet season supported more than half of the year's breeding by local reptiles. If rains fail for several years in a row, many species simply disappear from an area and may take decades to return, even when conditions improve.

E
Human activity is now putting these ecosystems under pressure. Grazing by farm animals strips away the thin plant cover that holds the soil together, and wind then carries the loose soil away. Water pumped from underground reserves for farms and towns lowers the water table, so that the roots of local trees can no longer reach it. In some regions, the spread of desert-like conditions into farmland, known as desertification, is made worse by the clearing of trees for firewood. Rising temperatures add a further risk, since many desert species already live close to the limits of what their bodies can bear.

F
Conservation in these regions is difficult but not impossible. Some governments have created protected areas where grazing is limited. In one project in the Sanrel region, local herders were paid to move their animals to new pastures every few weeks, giving plants time to recover. After six years, the plant cover inside the project area had doubled. Scientists emphasize that such schemes work best when local people help to design them, because residents understand the land far better than any outside visitor does.

items.q: A desert is defined mainly by its temperature.
items.vi: Đoạn A: sa mạc được định nghĩa theo lượng mưa, không phải nhiệt độ. Sai.

items.q: Some polar regions can be called deserts.
items.vi: Đoạn A: theo định nghĩa này, vùng cực cũng được tính là sa mạc. Đúng.

items.q: Cacti are the most common plants in hot deserts.
items.vi: Bài chỉ nói xương rồng lưu trữ nước, không nói chúng phổ biến nhất. Not Given.

items.vi: Đoạn C: nhiệt độ cơ thể lạc đà được phép tăng lên thay vì điều chỉnh bằng đổ mồ hôi. Sai.

items.q: The study in the Karrow Basin lasted ten years.
items.vi: Bài không nói nghiên cứu kéo dài bao lâu. Not Given.

items.q: Annual desert plants can flower within a few weeks after a heavy storm.
items.vi: Đoạn B: chúng nảy mầm, ra hoa và kết hạt trong vài tuần sau trận mưa lớn. Đúng.

options: It protects itself with sharp spines.
It stores water in thick stems.
Its roots spread widely near the surface.
items.vi: Đoạn B: rễ của cây tarsan lan rộng ngay dưới bề mặt để hứng cả cơn mưa nhẹ.

items.q: Where does the kangaroo rat get the water it needs?
options: From rain collected in its burrow
items.vi: Đoạn C: chuột kangaroo lấy nước từ hạt mà nó ăn nên không cần uống.

items.q: What does paragraph D suggest about long periods without rain?
options: Many species vanish from an area and return only slowly.
Birds are the first animals to disappear.
items.vi: Đoạn D: nhiều loài biến mất và có thể mất hàng thập kỷ mới quay lại.

items.q: What was the result of the project in the Sanrel region?
options: Plant cover doubled inside the project area.
items.vi: Đoạn F: sau sáu năm lớp phủ thực vật trong khu vực dự án tăng gấp đôi.

items.vi: Đoạn E: bơm nước ngầm làm hạ mực nước nên rễ cây không với tới được.

items.vi: Đoạn D: một mùa ẩm hỗ trợ hơn nửa số lần sinh sản trong năm của bò sát.

items.q: Which paragraph says that local people should help to plan conservation?
items.vi: Đoạn F: các dự án hiệu quả nhất khi người dân địa phương tham gia thiết kế.

parts.instr: Questions 27-40. Read the passage on the rise of public libraries and answer the questions.
parts.instrVi: Câu 27-40. Đọc bài về sự phát triển của thư viện công cộng và trả lời câu hỏi.

items.text:
A
The idea that anyone, regardless of wealth, should be able to read books free of charge is relatively recent. For most of history, books were rare and expensive, and libraries belonged to monasteries, universities, or wealthy families. Access was restricted to scholars and the privileged. Ordinary workers were often unable to read at all, and even those who could read rarely owned more than a single book. A person who wanted to learn about a new subject usually had to find a patient teacher rather than a printed page.

B
The change began in the nineteenth century, when industrial towns grew rapidly. Employers and reformers came to believe that education would produce more skilled and more orderly workers. In 1850, a law in the country of Eastmark allowed town councils to raise a small local tax to open libraries. The first libraries were modest: one room, a few hundred donated books, and a librarian who often had no training. Even so, attendance was high. A report from the town of Brindle recorded that the reading room was full by seven in the evening, with many visitors waiting outside.

C
Money from private donors helped the movement spread. A wealthy merchant named Alfred Penhallow paid for more than two hundred library buildings, but he attached a condition: the town had to promise to provide the land and to pay for the running costs. Critics at the time complained that this made councils dependent on one man's wishes, and some towns refused the offer. Supporters replied that the arrangement ensured that communities treated the libraries as their own responsibility rather than as charity.

D
Early libraries were not always welcoming. Many kept their books behind a counter, and readers had to ask a librarian to fetch each one. The rule was meant to protect valuable volumes, but it also discouraged people from browsing. This changed after reformers argued that readers learn best when they can handle the books themselves. By the early twentieth century, "open shelves" had become standard in most large libraries, and the number of loans rose sharply in the years that followed.

E
Libraries also changed who could use them. Children's rooms, first introduced in the 1890s, taught young people to value books and gave parents confidence that the library was a safe place. Later, many libraries started evening classes for adults, language lessons for newly arrived families, and lending services for people who could not leave their homes. A library, in other words, gradually became a community center as well as a store of books.

F
In the age of the internet, some predicted that libraries would disappear. Instead, many now report record numbers of visitors. Free computers and wireless networks have become among their most popular services, particularly for people who cannot afford a connection at home. Librarians also help visitors judge which online sources are reliable, a skill that is increasingly valuable. Several towns that closed their libraries to save money have since reopened them after complaints from residents.

G
Not everyone is convinced that the current model is sustainable. Funding is usually decided by local governments, whose budgets are under pressure, and some libraries have already cut their opening hours. Supporters point out that the cost of a library is small compared with the benefits it brings, such as improved reading skills among children and free access to information. The debate continues, but the survey evidence suggests that the public still values the institution highly.

items.q: Before the nineteenth century, most libraries were open to the general public.
items.vi: Đoạn A: thư viện thuộc về tu viện, đại học hoặc gia đình giàu, chỉ dành cho người có đặc quyền. Sai.

items.vi: Đoạn B: luật năm 1850 cho phép hội đồng thị trấn thu một khoản thuế địa phương. Đúng.

items.vi: Đoạn E: phòng thiếu nhi xuất hiện lần đầu vào những năm 1890. Sai.

items.q: Most of the first librarians were women.
items.vi: Đoạn B chỉ nói thủ thư thường chưa được đào tạo, không nói về giới tính. Not Given.

options: They wanted workers who would be cheaper.
They wanted to attract tourists to their towns.
They believed education would produce better workers.
They hoped to reduce local taxes.
items.vi: Đoạn B: họ tin giáo dục tạo ra công nhân lành nghề và có kỷ luật hơn.

options: To make the librarian's work easier
To protect valuable books, although it discouraged browsing
items.vi: Đoạn D: quy định nhằm bảo vệ sách quý nhưng làm người đọc ngại xem lướt.

items.q: What does paragraph F say about libraries today?
options: Most of them have closed permanently.
They remain popular and offer online services.

items.vi: Đoạn F: nhiều thư viện báo cáo lượng khách kỷ lục và cung cấp máy tính, mạng không dây.

options: Not interested in the future of libraries
Cautiously positive despite worries about funding

parts.instr: Writing Task 1. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. Write at least 150 words.
parts.instrVi: Bài viết 1. Dành khoảng 20 phút. Viết ít nhất 150 từ.

items.text:
The table shows the percentage of households with a home internet connection in four countries in 2005, 2015 and 2025.
Country A: 20% (2005), 55% (2015), 90% (2025)
Country B: 35% (2005), 70% (2015), 95% (2025)
Country C: 5% (2005), 30% (2015), 65% (2025)
Country D: 10% (2005), 25% (2015), 50% (2025)
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample: The table compares the proportion of households with a home internet connection in four countries in 2005, 2015 and 2025. Overall, access rose steadily in every country, although the starting points and the speed of growth differed considerably. In 2005, Country B had the highest figure, at 35 percent, followed by Country A with 20 percent. Countries D and C were far behind, at 10 and 5 percent respectively. By 2015, Country B had doubled its figure to 70 percent, while Country A reached 55 percent. Country C showed the fastest relative growth over this decade, rising sixfold from 5 to 30 percent, although it remained below the leaders. Country D grew more slowly, to 25 percent. In 2025, Country B was almost universal, at 95 percent, and Country A was close behind at 90 percent. By contrast, only 65 percent of households in Country C and 50 percent in Country D were connected. In summary, Countries B and A stayed in the lead throughout the period, while Country D fell furthest behind.
items.vi: Mô tả bảng số liệu: câu mở đầu diễn đạt lại đề, câu tổng quan, rồi so sánh các số liệu chính theo từng năm.

parts.instr: Writing Task 2. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.
parts.instrVi: Bài viết 2. Dành khoảng 40 phút. Viết ít nhất 250 từ.

items.q: Some people believe that working from home is better for both employees and companies. Others think it has serious disadvantages. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
items.sample:
In recent years, more and more employees have been able to do their jobs from home. While some people believe that this arrangement benefits both workers and employers, others argue that it harms teamwork and personal well-being. In my opinion, working from home is beneficial, provided that it is combined with some time in the office.

Those who favor remote work point out several advantages. First, employees save the time and money they would otherwise spend on commuting, which can amount to two hours a day in large cities. This time can be used for rest, family, or exercise, and as a result many workers report lower stress. Second, companies can reduce their costs by renting smaller offices, and they can recruit talented people who live far away.

On the other hand, critics raise valid concerns. New employees, in particular, learn a great deal by watching colleagues and asking quick questions, and this is much harder through a screen. Moreover, some people feel isolated when they work alone for long periods, and the line between work and private life can become blurred, so that they find it difficult to switch off in the evening. Managers also worry that creative ideas often arise from casual conversations in corridors.

Weighing these arguments, I believe that the best solution is a hybrid model. If staff work from home for two or three days a week and meet in the office on the others, they can enjoy the flexibility of remote work while still building relationships with colleagues. Companies that offer this balance are likely to have more satisfied and productive employees.

In conclusion, although working from home has some drawbacks, its benefits are considerable, and a flexible approach seems to be the most sensible way forward.
items.vi: Bài thảo luận hai quan điểm: trình bày cả hai mặt, nêu ý kiến riêng và kết luận rõ ràng.

parts.instr: Part 1. Answer the questions about familiar topics.
parts.instrVi: Phần 1. Trả lời các câu hỏi về chủ đề quen thuộc.

items.q: Let us talk about where you live. What is your hometown like?
items.sample: I come from a medium-sized town near the coast. It is quite quiet and friendly, and there are many small cafes and a big market in the center. I like it because everything is close, but young people sometimes find it boring.
items.vi: Câu trả lời nên mô tả quê hương và nêu lý do thích hoặc không thích.

items.q: Do you enjoy cooking?
items.sample: Yes, I do, although I am not an expert. I usually cook simple dishes such as noodles or soup at the weekend, because during the week I am too busy. I would like to learn how to bake bread.
items.vi: Trả lời có/không rồi mở rộng bằng thói quen và kế hoạch.

items.q: What do you usually do in the morning?
items.sample: I usually get up at six thirty, have a quick breakfast, and then take the bus to school. On the way I often listen to music or review my vocabulary. I do not like the morning very much, but I feel better after a cup of tea.
items.vi: Mô tả thói quen buổi sáng theo trình tự bằng thì hiện tại đơn.

items.q: How important is the weather in your daily life?
items.sample: It matters quite a lot. When it is hot and humid, I feel tired and prefer to stay at home, while on cool days I enjoy walking in the park. The weather also decides what I wear and whether I can play football with my friends.
items.vi: Nêu mức độ quan trọng của thời tiết và cho ví dụ cụ thể.

parts.instr: Part 2. Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2. Nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong một đến hai phút.

items.q: Describe a book that you enjoyed reading. You should say: what the book was about; when and where you read it; why you decided to read it; and explain why you enjoyed it.
items.sample: I would like to talk about a novel called The Lantern Keeper, which I read last summer. It is about a young girl who lives on a small island and looks after an old lighthouse after her grandfather becomes ill. During one stormy night, she rescues the crew of a fishing boat and discovers a secret about her family. I read it mostly at home during the holidays, usually on the balcony in the afternoon, when it was too hot to go out. I also finished the last chapters on a long bus journey to visit my cousins. I decided to read it because my best friend recommended it. She said that it was moving and also exciting, and she lent me her copy. At first I thought the story would be slow, but after the first chapter I could not stop. I enjoyed it for several reasons. First, the main character is brave but also realistic, so I could understand her feelings. Second, the descriptions of the sea were so detailed that I could almost hear the waves. Finally, the ending made me think about family and responsibility. I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes adventure stories.
items.vi: Trả lời đủ 4 ý của thẻ gợi ý: nội dung, thời gian và địa điểm, lý do chọn đọc, lý do thích.

parts.instr: Part 3. Discuss the questions about reading.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3. Thảo luận các câu hỏi về việc đọc sách.

items.q: Do you think people read less today than in the past?
items.sample: I think people still read a lot, but the way they read has changed. Instead of books, many people read short articles and messages on their phones. As a result, fewer people have the patience to finish a long novel, although some still read for pleasure.
items.vi: Nêu quan điểm rồi giải thích sự thay đổi trong thói quen đọc.

items.q: Why do some children not enjoy reading, and how could schools help?
items.sample: Some children find reading difficult or boring because the books they are given do not match their interests. Schools could help by letting students choose their own books and by organizing reading clubs, where children can share opinions with classmates. Teachers should also read aloud to make stories come alive.
items.vi: Nêu nguyên nhân và đề xuất giải pháp cho nhà trường.

items.q: Will printed books disappear in the future?
items.sample: I do not think so. Although electronic readers are convenient, many people enjoy the feel and smell of paper, and printed books do not need batteries. In my opinion both formats will exist together, with each one suited to different situations, such as traveling or studying.
items.vi: Đưa ý kiến về tương lai của sách in, có lý do và so sánh.
